What Aseprite is, and what this stage is.front: The versions this curriculum is pinned to
What Aseprite is, and what this stage is.back: **Aseprite 1.3.18.6-x64**, the Steam copy at `~/Games/steam/steamapps/common/Aseprite/aseprite`. **Aseprite Wizard 9.8.0.** **Godot 4.7**, GL Compatibility. **The art contract as reset 2026-09-22.** **Palette v0.1 — 132 entries in 33 ramps.** Config lives in **`~/.config/aseprite/`**; **no extensions are installed** and **only `default.ase` is in `palettes/`**, so the Shepherds palette has never been installed as a preset.

What Aseprite is, and what this stage is.front: Why learn all of Aseprite first
What Aseprite is, and what this stage is.back: **Habits are expensive to unlearn** — someone who learns the pencil and nothing else develops a way of working that routes around the features they do not know, and six months later the workaround costs more to replace than the feature would have cost to learn. **Two subsystems are prerequisites: Tilemap for terrain and Slices for 9-slice interface art.** **And it is small enough** — about eighteen manual pages, twenty-two lessons, a fortnight of evenings once.

The workspace.back: **The strip under the menus holding the options for the currently selected tool** — brush size, ink mode, pixel-perfect, tolerance, contiguity, selection mode. **It changes with the tool and nothing announces it**, which is why beginners never look at it. **If an option you need seems missing, you have the wrong tool selected.**

**§10.1: "Draw at native 1× resolution."** Everything looks good at 800% and nothing is decided there. **`1` zooms to 100% — the only level where a judgement may be made.** And **`F7` opens the Preview window: the sprite at 100% in a small floating window while you work zoomed in.** That is the answer to "how do I draw at 8× and judge at 1×", and keeping it open is the most useful habit in stage 1. **`F8` is the fullscreen version.**

Canvas, sprite and image.back: **Sprite** = the whole document: canvas size, colour mode, palette, layers, frames and tags. One `.aseprite` file is one sprite. **Canvas** = the rectangle the sprite occupies; changing it does not change what is drawn. **Image** = the pixels in a single cel, which is one layer on one frame. **Sprite Size resamples (the drawing changes); Canvas Size does not.**

**Internal viewport 960 × 540. A normal adult gameplay frame 112 × 112. Pivot (56, 96)** — bottom-centre, unless an asset-specific exception is deliberately approved. **About 80 px sole-to-crown**, with the approved idle measuring **81 to 87 px by direction**. **One world tile is 16 px with an 8 px subgrid**, giving about **45.7 px per metre**. Larger frames are permitted for large bodies, wide attacks and effects — **"Do not shrink a character merely to fit an effect."** (§4, §9.2)

Canvas, sprite and image.front: Why never to Trim a character master
Canvas, sprite and image.back: **Trim crops the canvas to the drawn content's bounding box, and the pivot is defined relative to the canvas.** Trim a 112 × 112 frame whose figure is 80 px tall and the pivot is no longer at (56, 96) — and **every frame will sit wrong differently**, because each has a different bounding box. The contract's own version: §4's **"Never normalize each frame's bounding-box height independently; doing so makes prone bodies grow."** **The canvas is 112 × 112 in every frame of every direction, and the figure moves inside it.**

Canvas, sprite and image.front: Why the pivot sits 16 px off the bottom
Canvas, sprite and image.back: **(56, 96) on a 112 × 112 canvas is the horizontal centre and sixteen pixels up from the bottom edge.** Those sixteen pixels are deliberate: **they are the room a pose needs to drop, a shadow needs to spread, and a frame needs for the feet to leave the ground without being clipped.**

Colour modes, and why indexed.back: **A pixel holds a number, which is a position in the sprite's palette** — not `#7C6D63` but "entry 7", with entry 7 holding `#7C6D63`. **Change entry 7 and every pixel using it changes at once.** RGB stores the colour itself (any colour); indexed stores an index (at most 256, exactly the palette's); greyscale stores value and alpha.

Colour modes, and why indexed.front: The four arguments for working indexed
Colour modes, and why indexed.back: **1 It makes palette discipline a property of the file rather than a rule to remember** — you cannot use an off-palette colour because there is nowhere to put it. **2 It makes the colour count visible**, so §10.1's bands are a glance rather than an audit. **3 A recolour is one operation** — four palette entries, not a hundred frames. **4 It forbids accidental anti-aliasing**, because a soft edge needs intermediate colours and there are none.

**Blending is constrained** — layer blend modes and opacity produce colours the palette may not hold, so Aseprite resolves them to the nearest entry and a 50%-opacity layer is not what you drew. **Index 0 is the transparent colour by default** (set in Sprite › Properties), so a visible colour must never sit there or it exports as holes. **And anything that interpolates** — blur, smooth gradients, resampling — **has nowhere to go.**

The palette.front: Installing the Shepherds palette as a preset
The palette.back: **The file is `media/reference/Palette/shepherds-master-v0-1.gpl`** — 132 entries, with a companion `.json`. **Load Palette** from the palette menu, then **Save Palette › Save as Preset**, which writes into **`~/.config/aseprite/palettes/`** and makes it available in File › New for every new sprite. **As of 14 October 2026 this had not been done** — only `default.ase` was there. **A palette you have to go and find is a palette you will sometimes not use.**

**The GIMP palette format: a plain text header plus one `R G B Name` line per colour.** Readable, diffable and the right choice for a palette under version control — which is why `colour-palette.md` keeps both it and a `.json` in the repository and names them *"the files to load in drawing and validation tools"*. **A sprite's palette is also saved inside its own `.aseprite` file**, so a master carries its colours and does not depend on the preset surviving.

The palette.front: Why the colour bar's width matters
The palette.back: **The palette is 33 ramps of four, in the fixed order `Deep → Shadow → Mid → Light`.** So the swatches run in fours, and **the colour bar's width decides whether you can see that** — set it so each row holds a multiple of four and the ramps line up as columns. **Then `9` and `0` walk along a ramp** rather than stepping randomly, which is what makes those keys useful.

The drawing tools.front: The five tools you will actually use
The drawing tools.back: **Pencil at 1 px (`B`)** — the overwhelming majority of every sprite, because an 80-pixel figure is built one pixel at a time. **Eyedropper held on `Alt`** — picking the neighbouring value is how a cluster grows. **Rectangular marquee plus Move** — shifting a limb two pixels, which is most of animating a 24-frame idle. **Paint bucket with contiguous on** — blocking in before shading. **Line, or `Shift`-clicked pencil** — the straight edges of props and architecture.

**The ink mode that paints along the palette rather than setting a colour.** Select a four-step ramp as the shading range and the pencil **moves each pixel one step lighter or darker** — left button one way, right the other. **With `Deep → Shadow → Mid → Light` ramps that is shading as a verb**, and it is the one Aseprite feature directly about the craft this curriculum teaches. The other inks: **Simple** (the default and the right one), Alpha Compositing, Copy Color, and **Lock Alpha** — paints only where something already is, so you can recolour without touching the silhouette.

The drawing tools.front: The tools that are traps on this project
The drawing tools.back: **Blur** invents intermediate colours. **The smooth gradient** is banned by §10.1's "avoid smooth gradients". **Spray** is exactly the "isolated noise" §10.1 bans. **Text** produces an image of text, where the game draws real text with a font. **Jumble** is a texture toy. All of them are study tools; none belongs in a master.

The brush, and the settings that must be.back: **A brush toggle in the context bar that removes the redundant pixel at each turn of a freehand stroke**, so a diagonal line does not leave **L-shaped doubled corners** that read as lumps. **On for lines and outlines, off when you want the doubled pixel** (deliberate anti-aliasing, some texture work) or when drawing single dots, which it can eat. **It fixes the doubled corner and not an uneven stair pattern — and an uneven stair is what makes a curve look wrong. The tool cannot do that part.**

The brush, and the settings that must be.front: The three settings that ruin a sprite quietly
The brush, and the settings that must be.back: **Any interpolation on a transform** — rotation and scaling can interpolate, inventing colours which indexed mode then quantises back to *almost* the right entry. **Nearest neighbour always.** **A non-transparent background layer** — it exports with the background, and the eraser paints the background colour instead of erasing. **Grid snapping left on** — useful for 16 px tiles, and it will move your two-pixel limb adjustment to the nearest grid line. **And one that should be on: the pixel grid, `Ctrl+Shift+'`.**

**Brush size, angle or colour varying with pressure, velocity or a stabiliser**, configured from the brush dropdown — new in the 1.3 line. **Turn all of it off.** A tablet with pressure dynamics on gives you a brush that changes size as you draw, which in pixel art is never what you want. **The hand does the work.**

Selection.back: **Move content by exact pixels — select, then arrow keys, one press one pixel.** That is how a 24-frame idle gets animated: a limb is selected and nudged, not redrawn. Also: **`F`** fills it; **a tool only draws inside it**; **`Ctrl+Shift+C`** copies the flattened result of all visible layers; **`Ctrl+Alt+N`** makes a new sprite from it; **Select › Selection as Grid** sets the grid from a marquee. Modes: **`Shift`** adds, **`Alt`** subtracts, **`Shift+Alt`** intersects.

Selection.front: The automatic outline, and why it is only a start
Selection.back: **Select the transparent area with the magic wand, invert, Select › Modify › Border by 1, fill** — a one-pixel outline in four operations. **And §10.1 bans "automatic double outlines" and outlines "that merge equipment into the torso", which is exactly what an automatic border does**: it cannot tell a satchel strap from a chest, and it closes the negative gaps the contract requires you to preserve. **It gets you 80% of the pixels and all of the wrong ones.**

Transformations.back: **Lossless: flip horizontal (`Shift+H`), flip vertical (`Shift+V`), and rotation by 90° or 180°** — every pixel moves to a new position and no colour changes. **Costly: rotation by any other angle, scaling that is not an integer multiple with nearest neighbour, and skew** — pixels do not rotate, they are resampled, and with interpolation on the result invents colours. **The rule: flips and right angles are free; everything else is a drawing decision you are asking the computer to make for you, and it will make it badly.**

Transformations.front: Why Shift+H is the most consequential keystroke here
Transformations.back: **Flipping is free, lossless, fast, and halves the work of an eight-direction character — and §5.4 forbids it.** *"Mirroring is permitted only for an explicitly approved asset whose handedness, costume and action geometry survive the flip."* Concretely: **Timon's reference ties limb colours to a side, so a flipped west would swap them**, and a character with a crook on one shoulder and a satchel on one hip has a handedness a flip reverses. **The industry normally draws five and flips to eight; the runtime supports both; the contract chooses one.**

Layers and groups.back: **§3.1: "Layers should separate only things that require independent editing or runtime treatment — body, equipment, shadow and effects — not every small colour cluster."** **Four layers, not forty.** Body (the base). Equipment (because it changes). Shadow (because the runtime may treat it separately, and a contact shadow is not part of the silhouette for the black test). Effects (because code may tint or hide them).

Layers and groups.front: Why a layer per material is a mistake
Layers and groups.back: **The silhouette becomes invisible** — you cannot judge a shape you are seeing in six pieces. **The outline cannot be drawn**, because a coloured one-pixel outline is a decision about what is next to what and requires seeing the whole. **The cel count multiplies** — 24 frames × 8 directions × 6 layers is 1,152 cels to keep in register. **And the export does it anyway**: Wizard's split-layer importer takes layers to separate textures, so if the runtime needs them separate, that is where it happens.

**Two or more frames sharing one image** — edit one and both change. Made by **`Ctrl`-dragging a cel** or Frame › Link Cels, and drawn differently in the timeline. **Useful for a held pose**: the approved idle holds its last pose from frame 10 through 24, which is one image rather than fourteen copies. **Dangerous for the same reason.** Note that **Timon's run reference uses byte-identical copies rather than links** for its two-frame holds — both survive export.

**Layer › New › New Reference Layer — an image shown behind the sprite for tracing or comparison, which does not export.** The right place for a reference frame, as against putting it on an ordinary layer and remembering to hide it. **The other layer kinds: normal (`Shift+N`), background (opaque, unmovable, and the eraser paints the background colour on it — character masters never have one), group, and tilemap (`Space+N`).**

Blend modes and opacity.front: Why blend modes are a trap on this project
Blend modes and opacity.back: **Indexed mode has nowhere to put a blended colour** — Aseprite resolves the result to the nearest palette entry, so Multiply at 60% gives you *some* entry chosen by distance, which is not a decision you made. **And what Wizard imports is the flattened image**, so any blend is baked in at export and can never be a runtime behaviour. **Runtime blending is Godot's job** — `CanvasItem`'s blend mode, `Light2D`, the sprite's material. **The working rule: layers in a master are Normal at 100%.**

Blend modes and opacity.front: The grey test as a toggle
Blend modes and opacity.back: **A new top layer, filled with any colour, blend mode Color, visibility off.** Turn it on and the sprite is greyscale; turn it off and it is not. **That is §10.1's grey test — "identifiable in grayscale" — made into one click**, and it is the most useful blend mode in the program for this project. Keep it in the 112 × 112 template. **All blend-mode use here is scaffolding**: it goes in while you work and comes out before the file is a master, because §3 deletes superseded material rather than archiving it.

The timeline.front: Aseprite has no frame rate field
The timeline.back: **Duration is per frame, in milliseconds, set with `P`** — and there is no sprite-level frame rate at all. **Playback speed is entirely a consequence of the per-frame durations.** So "12 fps" means a duration, and the contract's 12 fps means **84 ms** — not 83 — because of how Wizard converts duration to a frame rate on import. **And a longer frame is a hold**: a frame at 168 ms is two frames' worth of time in one cel, and it survives the import as a relative duration.

The timeline.front: Ranges, and why they do most of the work
The timeline.back: **Click a frame header and shift-click another for a frame range; drag across the grid for a cel range.** Then **nudging with arrow keys, transforms, copy and paste, deleting, reversing and linking all apply to the whole range.** That is the mechanism behind most animation editing here: shifting a direction's 24 frames one pixel left, reversing a swing to make its recovery, copying frames 1–10 to start another direction. **And `F6` turns on cel thumbnails, so the shape of a 24-frame animation is visible without playing it.**

Frames, durations and tags.back: **A tag is a named frame range**, holding a **name** (which becomes the animation's name in Godot), a colour (for your benefit only), an **animation direction** (Forward, Reverse, Ping-pong, Ping-pong Reverse), a **repeat** count, and user data. **Aseprite Wizard reads all of it**: the name becomes the `SpriteFrames` animation, the direction becomes the frame order with ping-pong expanded there-and-back, and a repeat count makes the animation non-looping.

**One master per asset, action and direction, named `<asset-key>_<action>_<direction>.aseprite`, carrying exactly one lower-case snake-case tag `<action>_<direction>`.** So `eli_idle_s.aseprite` holds one tag called `idle_s`. **Names state the action and direction plainly — `idle_s`, `move_ne`, `staff_attack_1_se` — and never sequence names like `animation1` or `walk2`.** (§3.1, §5.4) The redundancy is deliberate: separate files keep each direction independently reviewable.

**§5.3: "Locomotion and idle cycles loop. Attacks, interactions, reactions, downing and other one-shot actions do not."** So **loops have no underscore** — `idle_s`, `move_ne`, `graze_s`, `pace_w`. **One-shots do** — `_crook_attack_1_s`, `_dodge_e`, `_stoop_s`, `_death_se`, `_get_up_s`, `_sling_throw_n`. **The addon strips the prefix and inverts the default loop setting**, which is loop-enabled — so a prefixed tag imports with looping off. **Forget it and the character dies, and dies, and dies.**

**Tags can overlap and nest, and Aseprite permits it** — do not, because the contract says one tag per file and overlapping tags make the import ambiguous. **And a tag can be shorter than the sprite**: a file can hold 30 frames with a 24-frame tag, and only the tagged 24 import. Useful for keeping working frames beside a finished animation, **and dangerous because the untagged ones are invisible in Godot and easy to forget.**

Onion skin and playback.back: **The onion skin setting that makes frame 1's "previous" be frame 24**, so **you can see whether the loop closes.** With it off, frame 1 has no previous and the loop's seam is invisible while you work on it. **And here the seam is a deliberate feature**: the approved idle has a **3 px drop returning from frame 24 to frame 1**, seen in the preview and kept on purpose, with Timon rejecting evening it out. **So the onion skin's job is to show that yours matches the reference's, not to eliminate it.**

Onion skin and playback.front: The four conditions §5.3 requires, and where each is checked
Onion skin and playback.back: **"Every animation is checked at native scale, in motion, against the real ground and under representative lighting."** **At native scale** — Aseprite's preview window at 100%. **In motion** — Aseprite's playback (`Enter`, or `Shift+Enter` in the preview). **Against the real ground** — **Godot only**: a walk cycle that reads on a checkerboard can disappear against grass. **Under representative lighting** — **Godot only**, because `Light2D` changes value relationships. **An animation approved on Aseprite's checkerboard is not approved.**

Tilemap mode.back: Aseprite's own comparison: **a pixel holds an index / a cell holds a tile index; the palette holds colours / the tileset holds tiles; indices run 0 to N either way.** And the payoff row: **change a palette entry and every pixel using it changes — change a tile and every cell using it changes.** Edit one grass tile and every grass cell in the map updates. **Layer › New › New Tilemap Layer, or `Space+N`**, with the tile size taken from the grid — **16 × 16 here**, from §9.2.

**`Space+Tab` swaps them.** **Draw Pixels** edits the content of the tile under the cursor — you are painting artwork. **Draw Tiles** stamps tile references into cells — you are assembling the map, and the tile artwork is untouched. **The Tileset window** shows the layer's tiles with their indices and is where a tile is selected to stamp.

Tilemap mode.front: Manual, Auto and Stack — and the trap
Tilemap mode.back: The three pixel-drawing submodes. **Manual (`Space+1`): edits the tile in place and never reorders the tileset.** **Auto (`Space+2`), the default: creates or reuses tiles as you draw, and removes tiles that stop being used.** **Stack (`Space+3`): a new tile for every modification.** **The trap is Auto**: once a Godot `TileSet` references tile 37, an Auto-mode edit that removes an unused tile can renumber everything above it. **Auto while building; Manual once anything downstream knows the indices.**

**View › Tiled Mode — repeats the canvas in both axes as you draw, so a tile's seams are visible while you are making them.** The single most useful feature for terrain work. **And note that tiles may be stamped flipped or rotated, and Godot's `TileSet` supports flipped alternatives — so the no-mirroring rule does not apply to terrain.** §5.4 is about characters.

Slices.back: **A named rectangle on the canvas, with optional extra data** — not a layer and not a selection, but metadata that travels with the sprite and comes out in the export. **Tool: `Shift+C`.** Double-click to open properties, which hold **bounds**, the **9-slice centre** ("an internal rectangle to sub-divide the bounds into sub-slices"), a **pivot**, a name and free-text user data. **Slices are per-frame** — bounds can change frame to frame, and the exported data records the frame.

**The inner rectangle divides the image into nine regions. The four corners never stretch. The top and bottom edges stretch horizontally only. The left and right edges stretch vertically only. The centre stretches both ways or tiles.** So a 24 × 24 ornate frame can draw a panel of any size with its corners intact — which is what §8 requires with **"scalable borders"** and legibility at 1080p, 1440p and 2160p. **Godot's side is `NinePatchRect` and `StyleBoxTexture`, which take the same four margins the Aseprite centre rectangle defines.**

**Several images from one file** — one named slice each, then `--split-slices` or JSON from the sheet export. **A pivot**, recorded in the exported JSON. **A region for code** — a hit box, an attachment point, a text safe area — made machine-readable by the name and user data. **And keeping related interface pieces in one master**: `media/ui/map/` holds six separate marker PNGs, and one file with six named slices produces all six, in register and on one palette.

Saving, and the file formats.back: **`media/README.md`: "Exactly one authoritative editable `.aseprite` master per asset, action AND direction, and it lives here… If you find two editable masters for the same asset and family, that is a defect to resolve, not a convenience."** Masters go in **`media/sprites/<category>/<family>/<asset-key>/`** (categories: heroes, enemies, npcs, beacon, props, vfx, environment); generated sheets in **`_exports/`**, never hand-edited; **`media/reference/` is reference only and never holds a master**; `media/work/` is gitignored. **And §3: superseded art is deleted, not archived — no `old/`, no `v2` beside `v1`.**

**`.aseprite`/`.ase` keeps everything** — layers, frames, cels, tags, palette, slices, tilesets, user data, colour mode — and is the only editable master. **`.png`** keeps one image with alpha and loses layers, frames, tags and slices. **`.gif`** keeps frames and timing at 256 colours with one-bit alpha. **`.json`** is the sheet's metadata, written beside a sheet. **`.jpg` is lossy and invents colours at every edge — never for pixel art.** Everything that is not the `.aseprite` is a derived file (§3).

Export, and the sprite sheet.back: **Trim**: it crops each frame to its own bounding box and records the offset — **fatal here, because the pivot is (56, 96) relative to a 112 × 112 frame, so trimmed frames each sit in a different place.** Trim off; every frame is 112 × 112. **Scaling on export**: export at 1×, because the game does the scaling and §10.1 bans "resized or filtered source art". **A 3× export is a contact sheet to look at, not an asset.**

Export, and the sprite sheet.front: Why you mostly do not use the export dialog
Export, and the sprite sheet.back: **§3: "Accepted `.aseprite` masters import through Aseprite Wizard; no competing sprite export pipeline is established."** Wizard **invokes the Aseprite executable itself**, writes the sheet and JSON into the project and builds the `SpriteFrames` — which is why Godot's editor settings need `aseprite/general/command_path`, and why without it **every import silently fails with `valid=false`**. **The dialog is still for: a contact sheet to review, handing art to someone, understanding what Wizard does, and UI art — which is not sprite work.**

The command line.back: **`-b`/`--batch`** (no interface — the flag that makes the rest useful), **`-p`/`--preview`** (print what would be done; use it first, every time), **`--save-as`**, **`--sheet`** and **`--data`**, **`--sheet-type`**, **`--split-layers`/`--split-tags`/`--split-slices`**, **`--filename-format`** with `{tag}`/`{layer}`/`{frame}`/`{slice}`, **`--frame-range`**, **`--palette`**, **`--color-mode`**, **`--dithering-algorithm`** (none, ordered, old), **`--scale`**, **`--list-layers`/`--list-tags`/`--list-slices`**, and **`--script`** with `--script-param`.

The command line.front: Why the CLI is taught in stage 1
The command line.back: **It demystifies the import** — Wizard is a wrapper around these commands, and running them by hand once means the addon stops being a black box when an import fails. **It is the only way to inspect at scale** — a project will have hundreds of masters and the one-tag rule, the canvas size and the palette must be checkable without opening each. **And it is the foundation of validation.** Caution: **`--batch` with `--save-as` pointed at the input overwrites a master** — `--preview` first, always.

Preferences worth changing.back: **Auto-select layer: OFF** — on, clicking the canvas changes the active layer, and with four layers in register that moves the wrong thing. **Default interpolation: nearest neighbour** — the one setting that cannot be wrong. **Snap to grid: off** by default, on only while doing tiles. **Pixel grid: visible**, in a colour not in the palette. **Timeline thumbnails: on.** **Show full path in the tab: on** — you will have eight files called `*_idle_*` open. **Zoom with scroll wheel: on.**

Preferences worth changing.front: The canvas background is a judgement hazard
Preferences worth changing.back: **A mid-grey checkerboard makes dark pixels look lighter than they are.** Set the canvas background to a **flat colour**, and **change that colour while working** — a sprite that reads against both a light and a dark background is one that will read in the game. **And use a dark interface theme**: a light interface surrounding an 80-pixel sprite biases every value decision you make.

**Aseprite Wizard needs the executable path in Godot's EDITOR settings at `aseprite/general/command_path`.** On this rig it is the Steam install, **written out in full because Godot does not expand `~`**: `$HOME/Games/steam/steamapps/common/Aseprite/aseprite`. **Without a working path every `.aseprite` import silently fails with `valid=false`.** It is **machine-local and must never be committed.**

Shortcuts, and the hand position.back: **Hold `Alt` for the eyedropper. Hold `Ctrl` for move. Hold `Space` for the hand.** **Those three mean you never leave the pencil** — pick a colour with `Alt`, nudge with `Ctrl`, pan with `Space`, and the tool stays on `B` all day. **The single habit that most changes how fast the work goes**, and worth more than any other shortcut in the program.

**`B`** pencil · **`Alt`** eyedropper · **`Ctrl`** move · **`Space`** pan · **`1`** 100% · **`F7`** preview window · **`X`** swap colours · **`9`/`0`** step the palette · **arrow keys** nudge one pixel · **`P`** frame duration · **`F3`** onion skin · **`Shift+Enter`** play in the preview. **Read that list and notice what it is: draw, pick, nudge, pan, check at 100%, step the ramp, set the timing, see the motion. That is the whole job.**

**`B`** pencil · **`E`** eraser · **`I`** eyedropper · **`G`** bucket · **`M`** rectangular marquee · **`W`** magic wand · **`L`** line · **`U`** rectangle · **`V`** move · **`H`** hand · **`Z`** zoom · **`T`** text · **`D`** contour · **`Q`** lasso · **`R`** blur/jumble · **`Shift+C`** slice. With `Shift`: **`Shift+M`** ellipse marquee, **`Shift+B`** spray, **`Shift+G`** gradient, **`Shift+L`** curve, **`Shift+U`** ellipse. **All read from the shipped `data/gui.xml`, and rebindable at `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+K`.**

**Frames:** `Left`/`Right` step; **`,`/`.`** step within the tag; **`Alt+N`** new frame copying the current; `Alt+B` new empty; **`P`** duration; **`Enter`** play; **`Shift+Enter`** play in the preview; **`F2`** set the loop section; **`F3`** onion skin; **`F6`** thumbnails. **View:** **`1`** 100%, `2`/`3` for 200%/300%; **`Tab`** timeline; **`F7`** preview; `F8` fullscreen; **`Ctrl+'`** grid; **`Ctrl+Shift+'`** pixel grid; **`Ctrl+F`** advanced mode.

Extensions and scripting.back: **Extensions are packaged add-ons** — themes, palettes, sets of scripts — installed as `.aseprite-extension` files from **Edit › Preferences › Extensions**. **Scripts are single Lua files**, run from **File › Scripts**, living in **`~/.config/aseprite/scripts/`**. **As of 14 October 2026 neither folder exists on this machine** — no extensions, no scripts. **Which includes the Aseprite MCP Pro extension**: the server is registered in `.mcp.json` and has nothing to connect to, and it is an inspection tool for an assistant, not part of this curriculum.

Extensions and scripting.front: The six checks the palette validator should make
Extensions and scripting.back: The specification is already written in `colour-palette.md`. **1 Report every colour in a master that is not one of the 132.** **2 Accept four specific extras** — `#281E18`, `#241B16`, `#1F1F11`, `#FFFFFF` — which have no `TERR-` IDs and are not in the `.gpl`, and which *"a palette validator should accept, not flag"*. **3 Count the opaque base colours** against §10.1's bands. **4 Check the canvas is 112 × 112.** **5 Check there is exactly one lower-case snake-case tag.** **6 Check every frame's duration is 84 ms.**

**`app.sprite`** — the active sprite's `width`, `height`, `colorMode`, `layers`, `frames`, `tags`, `slices`, `palettes`. **`app.sprites`**, **`app.image`/`app.cel`/`app.layer`/`app.frame`**. **`Sprite(filename)`** opens a file. **`Image`** gives `getPixel`/`putPixel` and an iterator. **`Palette`** gives entries by index. **`Dialog`** builds a window with fields, so scripts can have an interface. **`app.command.*`** runs any menu command — how a script does something with no API. **`app.transaction`** groups edits into one undo step.

What the medium actually is.front: Why pixel art is not drawing small
What the medium actually is.back: **At high resolution a stroke is a gesture** — the tool averages thousands of samples into an edge and an individual pixel is meaningless. **In pixel art a stroke is a sequence of explicit decisions**: at 1 px with no anti-aliasing you placed every pixel and each one is visible. **One art pixel is 1.25% of an 80 px character's height and a 3 × 3 block on screen**, so a one-pixel error on an arm is a 3-pixel visible defect moving twelve times a second.

**The unit is the cluster, not the pixel** — a single isolated pixel reads as dirt. **A line is a run pattern** — a diagonal is a sequence of horizontal runs, and whether it reads depends on their consistency. **Value does the work and there is very little of it** — three or four per material, so a form is described by where a boundary falls, not by a gradient. **And everything is judged at 1×**, which is §10.1's first clause and the hardest discipline in the subject.

**Jaggies** — a diagonal with an uneven stair pattern, reading as a wobble. **Banding** — two value boundaries running parallel and touching, reading as a stripe instead of a form. **Noise** — isolated single pixels in a surface; §10.1's *"isolated noise"*. **Indiscriminate dithering** — a checkerboard used instead of a decision; §10.1's words again. **Two of the four are named in the contract; the other two are craft failures a contract cannot describe and a reviewer sees instantly.**

The cluster.back: **A connected group of pixels of the same colour** — the smallest mark that reads as a mark rather than an artefact. **§10.1: "Draw at native 1× resolution with deliberate clusters."** Four properties make one deliberate: **size** (two or three pixels is the practical minimum for a shape), **shape** (a cluster has a silhouette of its own — choose it), **edge** (the boundary with its neighbour is the drawing), and **intent** (you can say what it is for).

The cluster.front: Why a single pixel reads as dirt
The cluster.back: **The eye reads groups as shapes and isolated points as texture or error** — a lone highlight pixel says "there is a speck on my screen". **It is below the threshold at which a shape can be identified**, so it adds noise and no information. **And scale multiplies it**: at 3 × 3 the lone pixel becomes a 3-pixel block, now large enough to see and still too small to mean anything. **The exception: a point doing a job only a point can do** — an eye at 80 px, a rivet, a glint. **The test is whether you could name it.**

**Orphans** — single pixels not attached to a cluster, left behind by a freehand stroke or an eraser. **Fringing** — a ragged one-pixel border where the stroke wobbled; a cluster whose edge was not decided. **Confetti** — many small clusters of many values in a small area, where each may be deliberate and the result is still noise because nothing is large enough to read. **Confetti is the most common failure in a first character sprite**, and it comes from describing a form the way a painter would in a medium with four values and 1,350 pixels.

Lines: slope and the jaggy.back: **There are no diagonal lines in a pixel grid — there are steps, and a line is a pattern of them.** **1:1 = runs of 1 = 45°. 2:1 = runs of 2 ≈ 26.6°. 3:1 ≈ 18.4°. 4:1 ≈ 14°.** And the steep equivalents 1:2 ≈ 63.4°, 1:3, 1:4. **Those are the slopes a pixel grid draws cleanly and they are the only ones** — anything between has to be approximated, and the approximation is where jaggies come from.

Lines: slope and the jaggy.front: When a pixel line is clean
Lines: slope and the jaggy.back: **A pixel line is clean when its run lengths form a pattern you could predict.** `2,2,2,2` and `3,3,3,3` are clean; **`2,3,2,3,2,3` is clean because an alternating pattern is a pattern**; `2,2,3,2,2,3` is acceptable on a regular period of three. **`2,3,2,2,3,3,2` is a jaggy** — no pattern, so the eye sees bumps — **and nearly-predictable is worse than random.**

Lines: slope and the jaggy.front: The L-corner, and what pixel-perfect does not fix
Lines: slope and the jaggy.back: **Where a freehand stroke turns it often leaves two pixels at the corner**, one horizontal neighbour and one vertical, so the line appears to have beads on it. **Pixel-perfect mode removes the redundant pixel as you draw.** **What it does not fix is the run pattern** — it gives you a single-pixel line with jaggies instead of a doubled line with jaggies. **So the tool solves half the problem and the hand solves the other half: a clean line requires choosing the slope, not just drawing carefully.**

Curves.back: **If a straight line is a constant run length, a curve is a changing one — and run lengths must change monotonically, increasing or decreasing, never both.** `5,4,3,2,1` is a clean curve; `5,4,4,3,2,1` is clean (a repeat is fine); **`5,3,4,2,1` is a dent** because the 3-then-4 is a reversal and the eye sees the surface go in and out; **`5,4,3,4,3,2` is a lump.** **A reversal in the run pattern is a dent in the form**, and it is the commonest reason a hand-drawn curve looks wrong when nothing obvious is wrong.

**Two monotonic sequences meeting: runs decreasing to a minimum, then increasing** — for example `4,3,2,1,1,2,3,4`. **The point where the sequence turns is the inflection, and the eye finds it immediately — so put it where you mean the form to change direction.** **Most organic edges are S-curves**: a shoulder into an upper arm, a calf into an ankle, the back of a head into a neck. **Drawing them as two monotonic runs with a chosen inflection is the difference between a limb and a sausage.**

Curves.front: How to fix a curve that looks wrong
Curves.back: **Read it as runs, not as a shape — count the runs along the edge.** This is the single most useful habit: you stop seeing a wobbly arm and start seeing `4,3,4,2`, and then the fix is obvious. Also: **draw the extremes first** (the endpoints and the steepest and flattest pixels), so the run lengths have targets. **And use the curve tool (`Shift+L`) as a draft only** — Aseprite's answer is usually monotonic and usually too smooth.

Circles and ellipses.back: Rows, as run lengths: **d3** = a 3 × 3 square with the corners removed. **d4** = `2,4,4,2`. **d5** = `3,5,5,5,3`. **d6** = `4,6,6,6,6,4`. **d7** = `3,5,7,7,7,5,3`. **d8** = `4,6,8,8,8,8,6,4`. **d9** = `5,7,9,9,9,9,9,7,5`. **The sequences are monotonic to the middle and then mirrored** — the curve rule applied twice, which is why a circle that looks wrong almost always has a reversal in it.

**5, 7 and 9 have a single middle row and a clean centre pixel; 4, 6 and 8 have two middle rows and no centre.** **So for anything that needs an obvious centre — a wheel hub, an eye, the Beacon — use an odd diameter.** Above about radius 10, draw it with the Ellipse tool (`Shift+U`), which implements midpoint circle drawing, **then check one quadrant's runs for monotonicity and fix the two or three pixels at the 45° points where the algorithm's rounding shows.**

Banding.back: **Two value boundaries of equal slope running adjacent for their whole length, so the eye reads a band of colour rather than a surface changing value — and the form flattens.** **Line banding** is two single-pixel runs of different values side by side; the fix is to **widen one**, because a value needs more than one pixel of width to read as an area. **Edge banding** is two boundaries staying exactly parallel across a form; the fix is to **vary the distance between them** as the surface turns. **The principle: a value boundary should not be predictable from its neighbour.**

Banding.front: Why banding is invisible in your own work
Banding.back: **It looks tidy** — banding is the result of being careful, and neat parallel shading looks controlled while you draw it. **It is invisible at high zoom**: at 800% you see two clean lines doing their jobs, and at 100% you see a stripe. **And it is a global defect** — each individual pixel is right, and the error is in the relationship between two correct decisions, which is not where anyone looks. **Detect it by: 100% in the preview window, squinting, flipping with `Shift+H`, and greyscaling.**

Banding.front: Three contract clauses that are anti-banding rules
Banding.back: **"Approximately three or four purposeful values per major material"** — four values cannot band much, because more values means more boundaries and more chances for two to run parallel. **"Avoid smooth gradients"** — a gradient is banding taken to its limit, every boundary parallel to every other. **"Static shading stays restrained so Godot's local lights can read coherently"** — less shading, fewer boundaries, less banding. **The contract's reason is the lighting and the side effect is the craft.**

Noise against texture.back: **Texture: clusters of two or more pixels, in a pattern, drawn from the material's ramp, with density that varies with the form — and it reads as the material.** **Noise: isolated single pixels, randomly arranged, often several values or an off-ramp one, uniform in density — and it reads as an artefact.** **The test: could you say what the marks are?** "Mortar lines", "grain", "wool tufts" is texture. "It looked flat so I added some pixels" is noise.

**Dashes** — two- and three-pixel runs at a consistent angle, in the adjacent ramp step: wood grain, thatch, weave, long grass. **Blocks** with gaps: masonry, brick, cobbles. **Clumps** — irregular three-to-five-pixel clusters at varying density: moss, foliage, wool, rust. **Edge accents** — marks only at a form's boundaries, leaving the middle flat: the most economical texture there is. **A repeated motif**: scales, shingles, planks. **And the economy rule: texture the edges and the shadow, and leave the lit middle alone.**

**§10.1 bans "high-resolution texture imitation".** Concretely: **at 3 × 3 scale, grain drawn one pixel apart becomes a 3-pixel-period stripe pattern** that reads as moiré rather than wood — **and in motion it crawls**, because a texture finer than the movement between frames appears to swim across the surface. **The rule: a texture mark must be at least two pixels, and the spacing between marks at least two. Below that it is not texture, it is interference.**

Dithering, and where the contract bans i.back: **"Avoid smooth gradients, INDISCRIMINATE dithering, isolated noise and high-resolution texture imitation."** It does not say no dithering — it rules it out **as a default behaviour** and permits it as a decision. **And three facts make even deliberate dithering rare here: the scale** (a 50% checkerboard has a 6-screen-pixel period, large enough to see as a pattern rather than a tone), **motion** (the pattern is fixed to the sprite and the sprite moves, so it swims), **and the palette** — dithering invents a colour you do not have, and this palette has 132 entries in 33 four-step ramps.

Dithering, and where the contract bans i.front: The three legitimate uses of dithering here
Dithering, and where the contract bans i.back: **Large flat areas that must transition** — a sky, a big wall, water — where the alternative is banding across dozens of pixels. The area has to be large: over six pixels it is noise, over sixty it is a gradient. **A material whose appearance is genuinely speckled** — gravel, rough plaster, rust, sandstone — where the dither is texture rather than tone. **And a deliberate transition between two ramps** in a terrain tile, where a few rows of interleaving reads as a boundary rather than a cut. **Never on a character, never from a conversion, never from the gradient tool.**

Anti-aliasing, and why it is off.back: **It needs colours you do not have** — a step between Mid and the background requires something between them, and in indexed mode on this palette there is nothing between them belonging to that material. Plus: **an intermediate value is a new colour** against §10.1's 12–18 count; **at 3 × 3 an anti-aliased pixel is a 3 × 3 block of an in-between colour that reads as a fringe**; **baked intermediate values get tinted wrongly by `Light2D`**; and **a semi-transparent edge composites differently against every background.**

**Choosing the slope.** The problem anti-aliasing solves is an edge whose steps are visible; the pixel-art solution is **to make the steps consistent so the eye reads them as a line**. And if they are still visible, **the edge is at a slope the grid cannot draw cleanly — so move the endpoint by one pixel until it sits on a clean slope.** **That substitution is the whole craft difference: a high-resolution artist softens a bad edge; a pixel artist moves it to a slope that is not bad.**

**A long, nearly-flat curve on a large object** — a cart wheel, a barrel rim, a round hay bale at 53–65 px — where a single corner pixel of the adjacent ramp step can soften a visible step and the object is big enough to read as a curve. **UI art**, which §3 puts outside the sprite rules entirely: RGB PNG, no canvas or pivot rules, may be anti-aliased. **And dialogue portraits and illustrated scenes**, which §2 permits at higher resolution. **One pixel per corner, one ramp step, only where it is a problem at 100%.**

Selective outlining.back: **§10.1: "Use a dark coloured one-pixel outline. Avoid universal pure black, automatic double outlines and outlines that merge equipment into the torso."** Four requirements — **one pixel** (never two: at 80 px a two-pixel outline eats 2.5% of the height each side), **dark**, **coloured**, and darker than what it surrounds. Three prohibitions — **no pure black, no automatic double outline, and nothing that merges equipment into the torso.**

Selective outlining.front: Why the outline is never pure black
Selective outlining.back: **It reads as a hole** — pure black is darker than any material in the palette, so it becomes the highest-contrast element and the eye goes to it: the outline becomes the subject. **It flattens** — one outline colour says "cut-out"; a varying one says "form". **And `Light2D` cannot tint it**, so the sprite's edge stops responding to light while its interior responds. **The palette's answer: each material's own Deep step is its outline** — cloth `TERR-005`, leather `TERR-025`, metal `TERR-009` — with `TERR-001`–`004` for the deepest recesses.

**The lit side (upper-left): lighter, or absent** — a form turning into the light does not need a dark line, because the value difference does the work. **The shadow side (lower-right): darkest.** **Where two materials meet: the darker one's Deep step.** **Where a limb crosses the torso: a full dark outline, and a negative gap if there is room** — which is what makes the limb read as in front. **Against the ground, the contact shadow takes over and the outline can lighten.** The starting version: a full outline in each material's Deep step, then lighten along the upper-left.

Selective outlining.front: Four fixes for equipment merging into the torso
Selective outlining.back: **The failure: a satchel and the torso both outlined in the same dark colour with the outlines touching — the two lines merge and the satchel stops being a separate object.** **Fix one: a one-pixel negative gap**, which §10.1 requires anyway. **Fix two: outline the satchel and not the torso behind it**, so there is one line not two. **Fix three, and the best: make the satchel's value clearly different from the torso's**, so the shapes separate without the outline. **And the test is the black test — fill with solid black and see whether the satchel disappears.**

Pixel density, and consistency.back: **One world tile is 16 px; a normal adult is about 80 px representing about 1.75 m; so about 45.7 px per metre, with an 8 px collision and detail subgrid.** (§9.2) **That number is the density, and every asset is drawn at it.** And §9.2's separation of concerns: **"Footprint governs collision and placement; real proportion governs visible size. They are separate facts and every prop brief states both."**

Pixel density, and consistency.front: The three ways density goes wrong
Pixel density, and consistency.back: **Mixed source scales** — one asset at 1× and another drawn at 2× and scaled down, which has softer edges and more colours and sits in the scene like a photograph in a drawing. §10.1: *"deliberate clusters rather than resized or filtered source art"*. **Mixed detail scales at the same pixel scale** — a barrel with every stave against a crate of three flat values, so the detailed object looks closer or more important; the fix is §10.1's colour bands as a detail budget. **And scale drift in large assets** — checked by §9.2's **88 px clear door opening**, which an 80 px adult must fit through.

**Bucket 14–17 px. Crate 21–25. Firepit 10–13. Barrel 37–45. Square hay bale 19–23. Bench 19–23 seat, 46–56 long. Table 31–37 high, 55–70 long. Bed 21–25 high, 82–100 long. Round hay bale 53–65. Trough 23–28 high, 74–90 long. Cabinet 74–90. Cart 53–65 high, 100–120 long. Fence run 41–50. Dry-stone wall 50–60. Door opening at least 88 px clear.** **And §9.2's caveat: these are starting calibration, not approval — validate beside the real character at native scale and revise the table if drawn evidence shows a systematic problem.**

The detail budget.back: **A figure 81–87 px tall and 30–45 px wide is a bounding box of about 85 × 40 = 3,400 px, of which a human silhouette occupies perhaps half — about 1,600. A one-pixel outline is 200–250 of those. So about 1,350 interior pixels.** Divided roughly: **head 80–140** (10–14 px tall), **torso 350–450**, **each arm 120–160**, **each leg 200–260**, **a hand 8–20**, **a foot 15–30**. **About 1,350 decisions to make a person recognisable.**

**An eye is one pixel or none** — a 12 px head has room for about four pixels of face, and the reference's face mark is absent on back views entirely. **A hand cannot have fingers**: three pixels, a shape and a value. **A belt is one pixel tall, so a belt is a value change and not an object.** **A blade is 2 px wide**, which is why §10.1 lets signature equipment break the torso silhouette — sticking out is the only way a crook reads. **A fold in cloth is a 3-pixel dash and you get two or three of them, not twenty. Hair is a shape, not strands.**

The detail budget.front: The four things that carry identity at 80 px
The detail budget.back: **§10.1: "identity cannot depend on hue, glow, jewellery or microscopic detail"** — and a hero must be identifiable in solid black, greyscale, dark lighting and a busy party scene. **So: silhouette** (height, build, hair shape, hat, cloak, stance); **equipment shape** (the crook, the satchel, the sling — things that break the outline); **value structure** (which parts are light and dark, as a pattern); **and palette subset, which is the weakest, because identity may not depend on hue.** **Which is why stage 9 begins with silhouette and not the face.**

The 3× scale.front: What the delivery scale does to each defect
The 3× scale.back: **An orphan pixel becomes a visible 3-pixel block. A jaggy becomes a 3-pixel bump repeated along the edge. A banded pair becomes a 6-pixel stripe. A one-pixel dither becomes a 6-pixel chequer that shimmers. One-pixel-apart grain becomes a 3-pixel stripe pattern that crawls. A two-pixel outline becomes 6 screen pixels of dark border.** **Everything gets three times worse and nothing gets better** — the scale is a magnifying glass on mistakes and does nothing for the drawing.

The 3× scale.front: Judge at the delivery scale, not at 1×
The 3× scale.back: **The standard advice is "judge at 1×" and it is slightly wrong for this project: 1× is smaller than the player will ever see it.** The viewport is 960 × 540, so **1080p is exactly 2× and 2160p exactly 4×**, with the project's own working figure recorded as **one art pixel is 3 × 3**. **So judge at 300% in Aseprite**, with `F7`'s 100% preview as the secondary check — and in Godot for the two conditions neither can give you.

The 3× scale.front: Why animation works in single pixels
The 3× scale.back: **A one-pixel movement between frames is a 3-pixel jump on screen, and at 12 fps there is about a twelfth of a second between frames — so it reads as a jump rather than as a subtlety.** **A one-pixel difference between two frames is a real, visible movement.** Hence the approved idle's *"3–5 meaningful poses"* across 24 frames, and its deliberate **3 px loop drop**, which is visible precisely because 3 px is 9 screen pixels. **A limb nudged two pixels is a gesture.**

Reading your own work.front: Why you cannot see your own sprite
Reading your own work.back: **You have looked at it for forty minutes at 800%, placing pixels you chose — your eye has adapted, and your knowledge of what each cluster is for is doing work the drawing is not.** A reviewer seeing it for two seconds at 300% has none of that, **and their reading is the one that counts.** The six methods, cheapest first: **change the zoom, change the background, flip it, greyscale it, black it out, and leave it until tomorrow.**

**Set the canvas background to a flat colour and change it.** **Mid-grey** catches value errors — anything that disappears shares the background's value. **Near-black** catches the shadow side, which §10.1 requires to read *"in dark lighting"*. **Near-white** catches the light side and the outline. **And the actual ground colour is the real test, which happens in Godot** — a walk cycle that reads on a checkerboard can disappear against grass.

**In Aseprite: 300% and 100%; three backgrounds; flipped (`Shift+H`, then flip back); greyscale; solid black.** **In Godot: dark lighting, and a busy scene** — §10's seventh condition, *"the asset works in Godot under representative lighting, crowds and effects"*. **And then tomorrow**, which is the most effective of all and the only one that costs time. **§10's second condition builds in a second pair of eyes by design, and Timon's is a third with final say on design.**

Redrawing noise as clusters.back: **1 Count the values** — more than four is the first problem. **2 Reduce to two** — flatten the surface to its Mid, add only the Shadow. **3 Find the big shape** — one continuous boundary between light and shadow, following the form, and draw only that. **4 Add the Light**, only where the form faces the upper-left key, in fewer pixels than the shadow. **5 Add the Deep** only in the deepest recess and under an overlap — often not needed. **6 Stop.** **Step 3 does the work: a surface reads because of one clear value boundary, and everything else is decoration.**

Redrawing noise as clusters.front: What the black test proves about interior detail
Redrawing noise as clusters.back: **Compare a noisy surface and its rebuilt version in solid black: they are identical** — all that work was interior, and the silhouette carried the sprite either way. **Which means interior detail is never what makes a sprite read; it is what makes a sprite's material legible once it already reads.** In greyscale the rebuilt version has a readable value pattern while the noisy one is uniformly mid-grey; at 300% it has fewer, larger, more legible areas; **and it took a third of the marks.**

Fewer pixels.back: **Fewer, larger clusters. One slope instead of an approximation. A monotonic run sequence. Fewer value boundaries, and not parallel. Fewer marks, in a pattern. Choose a value instead of mixing two. Move the edge instead of softening it. Spend on silhouette, not detail. One boundary, then stop.** **Not minimalism as a style — it is what a medium with 1,350 interior pixels and four values per material can carry.**

Fewer pixels.front: Three checkable reasons fewer is better
Fewer pixels.back: **1 Legibility is a function of the largest shape** — the eye identifies an object by its biggest, highest-contrast features, and small features add competition rather than information. **2 Motion destroys small marks** — below about three screen pixels, anything that moves becomes shimmer. **3 Light destroys baked detail** — §10.1 restrains static shading *"so Godot's local lights can read coherently"*, and **every value you bake in is a value `Light2D` has to argue with.** The third is the project-specific one and the strongest.

Fewer pixels.front: The four questions to ask of every mark
Fewer pixels.back: **Can I remove this and lose nothing?** Then: **could I name it?** (if not, it is noise). **Does it survive greyscale?** (if it disappears when hue is removed, it was carrying no value information, and §10.1's grey test will fail on it). **Does it survive 300% in motion?** (if it shimmers, it costs more than it gives). **And the limit: fewer is not empty.** The order is silhouette, then the big value boundary, then material texture, then detail — **and the error this stage corrects is doing those in reverse.**

Why projection comes first.back: **"The projection is rectilinear three-quarter top-down, not diamond isometric. Vertical edges stay vertical; floors do not converge toward a vanishing point."** **Projection comes before value, colour and the figure because it is the only decision that cannot be fixed later** — a wrongly shaded barrel can be reshaded; a barrel in the wrong projection has to be redrawn. **And §9.3 lists projection first among the eleven checks every environment asset must pass.**

**"Every asset is checked for projection, visible scale, collision footprint, bottom-centre ground/Y-sort anchor, upper-left lighting, palette compatibility, silhouette at gameplay zoom, controlled detail, transparent isolation where applicable, contact shadow and absence of accidental damage or narrative wear."** **Modular pieces additionally pass repetition and corner seam tests, and interactive or destructible objects define their required states before drawing.**

The projections, named.front: The four projections, by their ground tile
The projections, named.back: **Top-down (plan): the ground tile is a square, vertical edges are a point — no height at all — and you see only the top.** **Three-quarter top-down: square tile, vertical edges vertical, and you see the top and the front.** **Isometric: the tile is a DIAMOND, verticals vertical, and you see the top and two sides.** **Side view: the tile is a line, and you see only the front.** **A square ground tile is the signature of Shepherds' projection — if you are drawing a diamond, you are in the wrong one.**

The projections, named.front: Where three-quarter top-down sits in the taxonomy
The projections, named.back: **It has no clean textbook name.** Honestly classified it is **a form of oblique projection**, closest to military or cabinet oblique, **and it is not geometrically consistent** — which is deliberate. **Perspective** converges (ruled out by §9.1). **Isometric** foreshortens all three axes equally at 120°, approximated in pixel art as **2:1 lines at about 26.57°** because a true 30° does not draw cleanly. **Cabinet oblique** draws depth at half length. Zelda, Stardew, Eastward, Sea of Stars and Shepherds are all three-quarter.

The rectilinear three-quarter top-down.front: Why the projection is not geometrically possible
The rectilinear three-quarter top-down.back: **A real camera tilted down would make the floor converge and the verticals lean. This projection does neither, so no single camera position produces this image.** **Which is the point: it is a readability convention.** A square grid means a tile is reusable anywhere on screen; vertical verticals mean a wall is reusable at any height; no convergence means an asset is correct at every position. **And §4 completes it — "The camera never rotates" — so there is exactly one view of the world.**

The rectilinear three-quarter top-down.front: The projection's inconsistency, and the ratio
The rectilinear three-quarter top-down.back: **The ground plane is drawn un-foreshortened — a 16 × 16 tile is a 16 × 16 square — and the top faces of objects standing on it ARE foreshortened.** That is inconsistent, and it is what makes the convention work: the floor stays a usable grid while objects read as having height. **The working rule: a box's top face is about half as deep as the box is wide, and every object in the game uses the same figure.** §9.3 checks for *"projection"* precisely to catch an asset that used a different one.

The rectilinear three-quarter top-down.front: Four questions to check an asset's projection
The rectilinear three-quarter top-down.back: **1 Are the vertical edges vertical?** No lean. **2 Is the top face foreshortened by the project's ratio, and the same ratio as every other asset?** **3 Are there any converging lines?** There should be none. **4 Is the ground footprint a square or rectangle on the 16 px grid, not a diamond?**

Why it is not isometric.front: The five reasons rectilinear beats isometric here
Why it is not isometric.back: **1 Movement and the grid agree** — in isometric, "up" moves the character diagonally, or the controls are rotated 45°; here §5.4's eight directions map onto the screen's own axes. **2 Square tiles tile trivially**, and Godot's terrain matching is built for square grids. **3 Y-sorting is one comparison** — depth order is screen Y — where isometric needs both axes. **4 Architecture is readable** — a straight run is straight and a corner is a corner. **5 Eastward and Sea of Stars, §2's named references, are both rectilinear.**

**Two sides plus a top is more information than one side plus a top, so objects read as more three-dimensional.** **Depth reads better over distance** — a long diagonal space has more apparent depth. **It suits tactical and building games** where seeing the footprint clearly matters. **And it is a beautiful look.** None of those outweighs movement, tiling, sorting and architecture here — **but know that when a tutorial teaches isometric, its box and tile geometry do not transfer.**

The implied camera, and the circle.front: What a flat circle looks like on the ground
The implied camera, and the circle.back: **In a true projection, a ground circle's height is its width times the sine of the viewing angle. Here there is no camera, so the ratio is a choice — and the working ratio is about half as tall as wide**: a 16-wide circular object is an ellipse about 8 tall. **It applies to every horizontal circular surface** — a barrel's top, a bucket's mouth, a well, a trough's end, a cauldron, a pool. **A vertical circle is a circle**: a standing cart wheel, a shield face-on, a round window.

The implied camera, and the circle.front: Why the Beacon is a circle
The implied camera, and the circle.back: **A sphere is a circle from every angle**, which is why §6.6 says *"Beacon is spherical and does not require character-style directional facings"*. **What makes it read as a sphere rather than a disc is the shading, not the silhouette** — the upper-left highlight and the lower-right form shadow. **And its contact shadow is an ellipse at the projection ratio on the ground beneath it: the shadow is what tells you the sphere is resting rather than floating.**

The box in projection.front: Which faces of a box are visible
The box in projection.back: **Front: yes, drawn true as a rectangle with vertical sides. Top: yes, foreshortened. Left and right sides: NO — that is the difference from isometric. Back and bottom: no.** **So a box's silhouette is a rectangle with a shorter rectangle on top, not a hexagon.** Construction: footprint in tiles → front face (footprint width × visible height) → top face (same width × footprint depth × the ratio) → join with vertical side edges → anchor bottom-centre.

**Where the top face meets the front face — the box's most important line, because it is the only thing separating the two faces.** **Without it the box flattens into one surface; with it too dark the box reads as two stacked objects.** The usual answer: **make the top face a lighter value than the front**, so the value difference does the separating and the line can be subtle. The box's whole value structure: **top lightest, front mid, any visible turned side darkest, contact shadow beneath — three values and a shadow, and the box is finished.**

The box in projection.front: A box's drawn height against its visible size
The box in projection.back: **A 1 × 1 object's total drawn height is its visible height plus its top-face depth.** A crate at 22 px visible height with a 16-wide footprint has an 8 px top face, so the sprite is **30 px tall** — and its *visible size* in §9.2's sense is the **22**. **The two numbers are different and the brief states both.**

The cylinder, the sphere and the cone.back: **Body: a rectangle, width = diameter, height = visible height, vertical sides. Top: an ellipse at the projection ratio. Bottom: a CURVE, not a straight line** — the bottom edge is the near half of an ellipse, so it bulges downward in the middle, and **getting this wrong is the commonest cylinder error.** Shading: top lightest; a light band left of centre; mid then shadow to the right; **and the value boundaries are vertical and parallel, which is textbook banding — so vary the band widths and let the boundary wobble at the staves and hoops.**

The cylinder, the sphere and the cone.front: Shading a sphere in four values
The cylinder, the sphere and the cone.back: **Concentric arcs, each at a chosen distance, with no dithering between them.** **Highlight: a cluster in the upper-left quadrant, about a third of the way in — not at the edge, not at the centre.** **Terminator: an arc concentric with the silhouette, offset toward the lower-right.** **Core shadow: the darkest band just inside the lower-right edge, not at the very edge.** A slightly lighter rim at the very lower-right edge if you have the value to spare — **and §10.1's restraint clause says you probably do not.** **Plus the contact shadow.**

**A triangle with a curved base** — the base is the near half of a ground ellipse. **Shading is radial**: the light and shadow bands converge toward the apex, so the boundary is a line from the apex to the base, left of centre. **The error to avoid is shading it with horizontal bands, which reads as a stack of discs.** Haystacks, conical roofs, piles, tents. **And a truncated cone — a bucket, wider at the mouth than the base — is the cylinder's construction with sloping sides**: at §9.2's 14–17 px that is two or three pixels of slope per side.

Height against depth.back: **The screen's vertical axis carries two of the world's three axes at once: moving up the screen means either further away (depth) or taller (height).** So **a 16-pixel vertical line is either a 16-pixel step northward on the ground or a 16-pixel-tall vertical surface**, and nothing in the geometry distinguishes them. **Four devices resolve it: the contact shadow, the visible front face, Y-sorting, and value.**

Height against depth.front: The four devices that resolve height against depth
Height against depth.back: **1 The contact shadow** — cheapest and most effective; a sprite with one is standing, without one it floats at an unknown height. **2 The visible front face** — a vertical surface shows one, a flat ground surface does not, **so a flat object must NOT have a front face or it reads as raised.** **3 Y-sorting** from the bottom-centre anchor — lower on screen draws in front, and the sort key is the anchor's Y, not the sprite's. **4 Value** — a top surface is lighter than a front surface, because the key light comes from above.

Height against depth.front: Decide height first, and draw it as a height
Height against depth.back: **Zero height** — a path, a rug, a scorch: **top surface only**, no front face, no shadow, no outline against the ground beyond a value change. **A few pixels** — a kerb, a step, a root: a thin front face and a contact shadow at its base. **41–60 px** — a fence or wall: a full front face, verticals, a contact shadow, a top face if thick enough. **Tall** — a tree or building: front face, **no visible top** because it is above the implied view, anchor at the base.

The 16-pixel tile and the 8-pixel subgri.back: **1 tile = 16 px ≈ 0.35 m. 3 tiles = 48 px ≈ 1.05 m — call it a metre. 5 tiles = 80 px ≈ 1.75 m — an adult's height.** A 1 × 1 footprint is 16 × 16 px of ground; a 6 × 3 cart is 96 × 48. **A door's 88 px clear is 5.5 tiles, so a doorway is six tiles wide in practice.** **And the 112 × 112 character frame is exactly 7 × 7 tiles**, with the figure five tiles tall and **16 px of clearance below the feet — exactly one tile.**

**Against the character, a tile is about a fifth of a person** — a believable paving slab. **Against the viewport, 960 ÷ 16 = 60 and 540 ÷ 16 = 33.75, so the screen is 60 × 34 tiles.** **256 pixels per tile** is enough for a material with four values and some texture and small enough that a terrain set is achievable. **32 would mean four times the drawing per tile and a coarser placement grid; 8 would not be enough for a material to read, and four times as many cells to author.**

The 16-pixel tile and the 8-pixel subgri.front: What the 8 px subgrid is for
The 16-pixel tile and the 8-pixel subgri.back: **Collision** — a barrel's collision circle need not fill its 16 px tile, so a 1 × 1 object can have a smaller collision footprint than its tile. **Alignment of detail** — a fence post every 8 px rather than every 16, a window centred on a half-tile, a doorframe's jamb. **Half-tile architecture** — a wall thickness, a step depth. **It is where footprint gets finer than the tile**, which is §9.2's *"Footprint governs collision and placement"* made workable.

45.7 pixels per metre.back: **80 px ÷ 1.75 m = about 45.7 px per metre** (§9.2). Forward: **10 cm ≈ 5 px; 25 cm ≈ 11; 50 cm ≈ 23; 1 m ≈ 46; 1.5 m ≈ 69; 2 m ≈ 91.** **Reverse, and this is the one you use more: 1 px ≈ 2.2 cm; 8 px ≈ 17 cm; 16 px ≈ 35 cm.** **Hold the 2.2 cm figure** — it makes the detail budget concrete: a hand is 2–3 px because a hand is 6–8 cm across, and an eye is 1 px because an eye is 2–3 cm. **One pixel genuinely is about the size of a thumbnail.**

45.7 pixels per metre.front: How to size something not in the table
45.7 pixels per metre.back: **1 Find the real object's size in metres** — a shepherd's crook is about 1.5 m; a sheep about 1.2 m long and 0.9 m at the shoulder. **2 Multiply by 45.7** — the crook is 69 px, the sheep 55 px long and 41 at the shoulder. **3 Sanity-check against the figure** — the crook at 86% of adult height looks right. **4 Adjust for readability DELIBERATELY and record that you did**, because §9.2 separates footprint from visible size and §10.2 requires the brief to state both. **Real proportion is the starting point; readability wins.**

Footprint against visible size.back: **§9.2, stated twice: "Footprint governs collision and placement; real proportion governs visible size. They are separate facts and every prop brief states both."** **Footprint** is the ground rectangle in tiles, governing collision, placement, Y-sorting and walkability — used by the engine and the level designer. **Visible size** is how big the drawn sprite is in pixels, governing how big the thing looks — used by the eye.

Footprint against visible size.front: The two errors the footprint separation prevents
Footprint against visible size.back: **Sizing the sprite from the footprint** — a 1 × 1 barrel drawn 16 px tall because its footprint is 16 px, when a real barrel is 37–45 px. **The footprint is the ground, not the height.** **Sizing the footprint from the sprite** — a cart drawn 110 px long given a 7-tile footprint, when §9.2 says 6 × 3 because the shafts overhang and a player should be able to walk past them. **The second is the more annoying in play: invisible collision where the sprite looks like empty space.**

Footprint against visible size.front: The eight fields of an asset brief
Footprint against visible size.back: **§10.2: "Before drawing, an asset brief identifies its subject, states, directions, actions, frame geometry, anchor, palette subset and runtime consumer."** For a bucket: subject (a domestic wooden pail, York); footprint 1 × 1; visible size 15 px high; frame geometry (its own size plus room for the shadow — **not 112 × 112**, which is the character frame); anchor bottom-centre; palette subset **4–10 colours** from the wood and metal ramps; states — one, static; runtime consumer — a placed prop in the York scene.

The ground anchor and the contact shadow.back: **The anchor is a point on the canvas and the drawing has to be placed relative to it** — a bucket drawn in the middle of its canvas with the anchor at the canvas's bottom-centre **will float.** **The object's lowest ground-touching pixel sits at the anchor's row, centred on the anchor's column.** For a character at **(56, 96)** that means the soles are at row 96, **with 16 rows of canvas below them** — the clearance a jump or a crouch needs. §4: *"Collision and gameplay origin remain at the feet."*

The ground anchor and the contact shadow.front: How to draw a contact shadow
The ground anchor and the contact shadow.back: **Shape: an ellipse at the projection ratio matching the footprint** — a 1 × 1 object gets about 14 wide by 5–7 tall. **Position: centred on the anchor, extending a pixel or two beyond the base on the lower-right and barely at all on the upper-left**, because the key light is upper-left. **Value: one or two steps darker than the ground, usually a dark neutral from `TERR-001`–`004`**, which the palette lists for *"contact accents"*. **Edges hard.** **Its own layer**, per §3.1 — so the runtime can treat it separately and the black test can exclude it.

**1 It resolves height against depth** — with one the sprite is standing, without one it floats at an unknown height. **2 It separates the object from the ground's value**, so a mid-value barrel on mid-value earth still reads. **3 It anchors motion** — §4's *"Ground contact must be stable in every frame"*, and a shadow that stays put while the body moves is how that reads. **And a jumping character's shadow stays on the ground and shrinks; it does not travel up with the body.**

Consistency across assets.front: The five things that must match across assets
Consistency across assets.back: **1 The top-face ratio** — one crate's top at half depth and the next at two-thirds read as being seen from different heights. **2 The key light direction** — upper-left, always (§10.1); an asset lit from the upper-right reads as glowing. **3 The pixel density** — 45.7 px per metre and the same detail budget per asset class. **4 The palette** — §9.3's *"palette compatibility"*; two stone objects from two different ramps are not the same stone. **5 The contact shadow's treatment** — a darker or longer shadow sits the object at a different height.

**A character silhouette at 80 px, a 16 px grid, a 1 × 1 and a 2 × 2 footprint, a shaded reference box at the project's top-face ratio, and a contact shadow** — used as a **reference layer** in every new asset file. **§9.2's own instruction: "Validate them beside the real character at native scale."** **A file and not a memory, because the ratio is a number you will not remember in three weeks and a drawn reference does not drift.**

**The first asset sets the standard and the first asset is the worst one you will draw** — so either everything matches it and the whole set is weak, or the set drifts as you improve. **The answer is §3's: "Rejected and superseded art is deleted rather than archived." Redraw the early ones.** The contract expects it, since nothing is approved until Master Roachi approves the actual asset. **Expect to redraw the first three or four props and the first character, and budget for it rather than defending them.**

The seven projection failures.back: **1 Reads as isometric** — two side faces, or a diamond footprint. **2 Converging or leaning edges** — a vertical drawn at a slope. **3 The wrong top-face ratio**, including a top face not foreshortened at all. **4 No top face where there should be one, or one where there should not** — a flat ground marking with a front face reads as raised. **5 A baked floor or cast shadow** — against §9.1's *"Do not bake a floor"*. **6 The anchor not at the bottom-centre of the ground contact** — which makes the object sort wrongly. **7 Scale drift.**

The seven projection failures.front: The one diagnostic that catches six of the seven
The seven projection failures.back: **Put the asset next to an 80-pixel character silhouette, a 16 px grid and an accepted reference box, at 300%.** Isometric is obvious immediately; leaning verticals against the grid; the wrong ratio against the reference box; a missing or wrong top face; a baked floor against a different ground; scale drift against the figure. **The one it does not catch is the anchor** — that needs Godot or a measurement, and from stage 1, **trimming a frame moves it, so that failure is often an export setting rather than a drawing.**

Why value before colour.back: **Nine of its ten clauses are about value** — four values per material, the upper-left key, identifiable in solid black, in greyscale, in dark lighting, in a busy scene, negative gaps, a dark outline — **and one says identity may not depend on hue at all.** Only the 12–18 colour band is about colour. **Value carries form, depth, separation and readability; hue carries identity and mood and almost nothing else.**

**1 Silhouette, in one value — the black test lives here. 2 The big value boundary, where light becomes shadow across the whole form. 3 The third and fourth values — Light where it faces the key, Deep in recesses. 4 Then hue: which ramp each material takes. 5 Then the outline. 6 Then material texture, and stop.** **Steps 1–3 are stage 4, step 4 is stage 5, step 6 is stage 6 — and drawing in this order is the single biggest practical change this curriculum asks for, because the instinct is to pick colours first.**

Why value before colour.front: Why value matters more in this medium specifically
Why value before colour.back: **Scale** — at 80 px a character has no detail that is not a value boundary. **The crowd** — §2 requires readability in *"movement, combat, crowds, darkness and effects"*, and in a crowd hue is noise while value separates. **The lighting** — `Light2D` changes hue and saturation freely and compresses value, so a sprite whose readability is in hue stops reading. **And the palette** — it is built as `Deep → Shadow → Mid → Light` ramps, so **the tool the project gives you is a value tool.**

The four-value material.front: The four values and their proportions
The four-value material.back: **Mid** — the material's local colour, the default and largest area: **50–60%**. **Shadow** — where the surface turns away from the key light: **25–35%**. **Light** — where it faces the key directly: **10–15%**. **Deep** — recesses, undersides, contact points and the outline: **5–10%**. **Those proportions are the lesson** — the commonest beginner distribution is roughly equal quarters, which produces a sprite with no dominant value and therefore no read. **A material is mostly its Mid.**

**Shadow is a form shadow: the surface is turned away from the light, and it is a function of DIRECTION.** **Deep is occlusion: light cannot reach because something is in the way, and it is a function of PROXIMITY.** So **the right side of a cylinder is Shadow; the crevice where two cylinders touch is Deep — and it is Deep on both of them, including on the lit side.** **A sprite with Deep only on the shadow side looks flat; one with Deep in the crevices reads as solid.**

**"Does this face up or toward the upper-left?" → Light. "Does this face the viewer?" → Mid. "Does this face away from the upper-left?" → Shadow. "Is something else in the way of the light here?" → Deep.** **Ask them in that order on every surface and the shading is determined.** The art is deciding what "faces up" means for a cluster three pixels across. **And note you do not choose four values — you choose a ramp, and the four come with it.**

Why three or four, and not six.front: The colour bands divided by four
Why three or four, and not six.back: **A small prop at 4–10 colours ÷ 4 values = one to two and a half materials. A hero at 12–18 = three to four and a half. An ordinary enemy at 8–26 = two to six.** **So a hero gets three or four materials — skin, cloth, leather, metal — and that is the budget.** **The four-value rule and the colour band are the same rule stated twice**, and either implies the other. `colour-palette.md` is tighter still: enemies about 8–14, heroes about 12–18.

Why three or four, and not six.front: The four reasons for three or four values
