A prop with a state.back: **Option A — two files, two Static Textures**: `wooden-pail_upright.aseprite` and `wooden-pail_fallen.aseprite`, treating the state as the *action* slot in §3.1's grammar. **Each state is independently reviewable; the anchors must match exactly.** **Option B — one file, two tags, a `SpriteFrames`**: `upright` and `_fallen`, the underscore making the fallen state a one-shot. **One anchor, guaranteed register; but it is a `SpriteFrames` for something unanimated.** **The rule: a state reached instantly → two textures; a state reached through a transition → one animation with the `_` prefix.**

What the round trip taught.back: **1 Brief. 2 Silhouette, one value, black test. 3 Value — two then three then four, upper-left key. 4 Colour — a ramp per material, within the band. 5 Outline and contact shadow, selective, own layers. 6 Checks — greyscale, black, beside the figure. 7 Name and place — the path, the one-master rule. 8 Import — the right importer, the excluded layers. 9 Godot — real scene, real ground, real zoom, a light. 10 §10's eight conditions.** **After three props these take about as long as step 3 alone.**

What the round trip taught.front: The five numbers that travel with every asset
What the round trip taught.back: **The canvas. The anchor — bottom-centre of the ground contact, a fixed distance above the canvas bottom. The footprint, in tiles. The visible size, in pixels, against §9.2's band. The colour count, against §10.1's band.** **Write them on the master's own layer, or in the brief: an asset whose five numbers are recoverable can be checked; one whose numbers are in your head cannot.**

**1 Drawing decisions get feedback** — before this stage every value decision was a guess about how it would look in the game; now it is a question with an answer ten minutes away, **which is why stage 4's restraint clause only becomes real here.** **2 The checks become cheap and therefore get run.** **3 The scary assets get smaller** — a character is 192 drawings and one pipeline, and the pipeline is now free. **And the two limits: the bucket is not a production asset, and nothing has been approved — condition 2 is a separate event only Master Roachi can satisfy.**

What a tile has to do.front: Why a tile is not a prop
What a tile has to do.back: **The viewport is 60 × 34 tiles — about 2,040 placements on screen, and 10,000 to 50,000 across a scene — all of them the same 256 pixels. So a one-pixel error in a ground tile is a one-pixel error repeated two thousand times.** Four requirements a prop does not have: **it must tile seamlessly; it must not produce a pattern when repeated; it must be quiet (the floor is the largest area and should be the least interesting); and it must connect to its neighbours.**

What a tile has to do.front: What §9 leaves open for environment art
What a tile has to do.back: **§9's first line: "No current terrain, prop, building, character-effect or environment art is approved."** **And §9.3's close: "Terrain transition grammar, environment material ramps, final York calibration assets, destruction states and VFX rules remain open work. Implementation placeholders do not approve visual style."** **So this stage teaches how transition grammars work and what each option costs — not which one Shepherds uses, because that has not been decided.**

The sixteen-pixel tile, authored.front: Turn on Tiled Mode before drawing, not after
The sixteen-pixel tile, authored.back: **Drawing a tile with Tiled Mode off and checking it afterwards is backwards** — you will have made edge decisions that do not work. **With `View › Tiled Mode` on from the start, every mark is immediately visible in its tiled context and the edges take care of themselves.** **And it lets you draw across the tile boundary, wrapping the stroke, so a mark that crosses an edge is split correctly for free.**

The sixteen-pixel tile, authored.front: The seam test, and the cheap answer
The sixteen-pixel tile, authored.back: **Does the tile's right edge meet its own left, and its bottom its top, without a visible line? Check in Tiled Mode at 300%.** A failure shows as **a visible grid**. Two causes: **a mark touching an edge with no counterpart on the opposite edge**, or **a value imbalance between edges**. **And the cheap answer: keep every mark at least two pixels from every edge, and the seam test becomes automatic** — it costs a little variety and it is worth it. **The budget: two values, three to five marks, under 10% of the tile marked.**

Variants and the repetition test.front: The repetition test against the seam test
Variants and the repetition test.back: **The seam test asks whether the edges meet. The repetition test asks whether the tiled field reads as a surface or as a grid of repeated units** — tile it 8 × 8 and look at the whole thing. **A tile can pass the seam test perfectly and still produce an obvious grid, because what repeats is not the edge but the content.** **The honest check: does it look like ground, or like a tilemap? If you can count the tiles, it fails.**

Variants and the repetition test.front: The three ways to break a tile pattern
Variants and the repetition test.back: **1 Make the single tile quieter** — a tile with no distinctive mark cannot produce a lattice; two values and three marks is the practical floor. **2 Variants, placed randomly** — three to five, differing only in the marks' POSITIONS, never in overall value, **which reduces the lattice's period from 1 tile to about 4, or 64 px.** **3 Scatter objects on top** — tufts, pebbles, cracks as separate placeables at one in eight to twenty, **which works better because the scatter is at a different frequency from the grid.**

Godot's TileSet, and terrain sets.back: **Each tile carries bits for its neighbours. `-1` means empty space or no terrain; `0` or greater is a terrain ID. A tile is chosen when its neighbours match its bits** — the docs' example: *"a tile with all peering bits set to `0` or higher appears only if all 8 neighbouring tiles are using a tile with the same terrain ID"*, and *"if top-adjacent bits are set to `-1`, it will only appear if there is empty space on top of it (including diagonally)"*. **So you paint "grass" and Godot picks which grass tile. That is autotiling.**

Godot's TileSet, and terrain sets.front: The three terrain modes, and their tile cost
Godot's TileSet, and terrain sets.back: **Named exactly as the editor names them: Match Corners and Sides (all eight neighbours), Match Corners (the four diagonals), Match Sides (the four orthogonals).** The Godot docs map them to Godot 3's 2 × 2, 3 × 3 and 3 × 3-minimal bitmask modes without saying which is which. **The tile counts for full coverage are practical knowledge rather than documented: Match Sides 16, Match Corners 16, Match Corners and Sides 47 — the "blob" set, 256 raw combinations reducing to 47.**

**16 tiles is a day's work; 47 is a week's.** **York's terrain boundaries are mostly simple** — a path across grass, a wall's base — **and inner corners are rare.** **And §9.3 leaves the grammar open, so the first terrain set is a proposal: draw 16, use them, and find out whether the missing cases matter.** What Match Sides gives up: **edges and outer corners, but no inner corners — a boundary that turns inward has a visible notch.**

Transition grammar.back: **A hard cut** — the two materials simply abut; **no extra tiles.** **An edge set** — a dedicated tile per boundary configuration; **16 or 47 per pair.** **An overlay** — a transparent tile on a second `TileMapLayer` carrying the boundary; **16 or 47 per material, reusable over any base.** **The arithmetic: six ground materials with dedicated sets is 6 × 5 = 30 transitions × 16 = 480 tiles. Overlays are 6 × 16 = 96. That is the difference between a feasible terrain set and an infeasible one.**

Transition grammar.front: The 16 tiles of a Match Sides edge set
Transition grammar.back: **1 tile: all four sides the same — the interior fill (already drawn). 4: one side foreign — the straight edges N, E, S, W. 4: two adjacent sides foreign — the outer corners. 2: two opposite sides foreign — the one-tile strips, horizontal and vertical. 4: three sides foreign — the strip ends. 1: all four foreign — an isolated tile. Sixteen.** **Draw them in that order, because each group is a variation on the last.**

Transition grammar.front: Three rules for drawing an edge
Transition grammar.back: **1 The edge is a shape, not a line** — grass meeting earth is a ragged two-or-three-pixel incursion, **and a straight boundary reads as a mown lawn.** **2 The edge carries the occlusion** — a one-pixel darker line on the lower material's side where the upper overlaps, **which is what makes grass look like it is growing over earth rather than printed beside it.** **3 The edge must not create a pattern** — the ragged incursion should differ on each of the four straight edges, and ideally there are two variants of each.

Authoring a terrain set in Aseprite.back: **One file as a grid of 16 × 16 cells — a 4 × 4 arrangement at 64 × 64, or an 8 × 4 sheet with the second half empty so the set can grow.** **The whole set is visible, the seam tests are runnable, there is one file to import, and the tile indices are positional and stable.** **And the one-master rule is satisfied: the sheet IS the asset** — a terrain set is one thing. **Sixteen separate files would mean assembling them constantly, because the tests require the set.**

**Godot reads a `TileSetAtlasSource` as a grid, so a tile's identity is its position in the sheet — which means once a `TileSet` references the tile at (2, 1), moving that tile breaks the TileSet.** **Decide the layout first and write it down.** And **Aseprite's Tilemap mode and Godot's `TileSet` are different things**: Aseprite's is an authoring convenience (edit a tile once and every cell updates — useful for mocking up a scene), Godot's is the runtime structure. **Manual submode (`Space+1`) once anything downstream knows the indices.**

The Tileset Texture importer.front: Master to painted tiles, in ten steps
The Tileset Texture importer.back: **1 The sheet in `media/sprites/environment/<family>/<asset-key>/`. 2 Import tab, set the importer to Tileset Texture, Reimport. 3 A `TileSet`. 4 Add a `TileSetAtlasSource` with the texture. 5 Tile size 16 × 16, separation and margins zero. 6 Create tiles. 7 A terrain set in Match Sides mode. 8 Set each tile's peering bits. 9 A `TileMapLayer` with that `TileSet`. 10 Paint with the terrain brush.** **Step 8 is the laborious one, and it is where the layout decision pays off.**

The Tileset Texture importer.front: The terrain bits survive a reimport
The Tileset Texture importer.back: **The peering bits live on the `TileSet`, not on the texture — so you can redraw the sheet and reimport and the terrain assignments survive, as long as the tile positions have not moved.** **Which is the whole reason the layout is a contract.** **And the importer does not do collision either** — a `TileSet` holds collision shapes per tile, set in Godot, which is where §9.2's 8 px subgrid applies. Four things that go wrong: **the tile size is not 16; the sheet has separation or margins; transparent tiles get skipped by "create tiles in non-transparent regions"; and the indices shift.**

Modular architecture: the four tests.back: **§9.1 names three and §9.3 adds the fourth.** **1 Straight run** — place the piece five times in a row: do the joints disappear, is the run continuous? **2 Corner** — turn the run 90 degrees: is there a corner piece, and does it work as both an outer and an inner corner? **3 Transition seam** — where the piece meets a different material or piece, like a wall meeting a door frame. **4 Repetition** — does the five-piece run read as a wall, or as five copies? **Run them in that order, because each can invalidate the next.**

Modular architecture: the four tests.front: Hide the modular joint inside the material's structure
Modular architecture: the four tests.back: **A piece's right edge meets the next piece's left, and any asymmetry shows as a repeating vertical line. The two edges must be complementary — a block that ends halfway at the right continues at the left.** **And the structural answer: make the joint fall where a joint belongs.** Brick courses, plank ends, fence posts, roof tile overlaps — **all are natural places for a seam, and a piece whose boundary falls there has no visible seam at all.** **Piece size: two tiles (32 px) is the compromise — the repetition period doubles and it is still placeable anywhere.**

**A straight section; an outer corner; an inner corner; an end cap; a top or coping if the wall is thick enough to have a top face; and two or three variants of the straight section for the repetition test.** **Six to nine pieces for one wall material, which is the honest cost of modularity.**

Walls.back: **The coping or top: lightest, because it faces up. The front face: Mid, the largest area. The vertical ends: Shadow on the right, Mid on the left. And the base: a one-or-two-pixel line of Deep where the wall meets the ground.** **That base line is the single most valuable pixel row in architecture** — stage 4's *"one pixel of Deep along the base does more for an interior than any amount of wall texture"*.

Walls.front: Where each wall type's joint belongs
Walls.back: **Dressed masonry: a mortar line — end the piece mid-course with a staggered edge. Dry-stone: between two blocks, irregularly — easy, because the material is irregular. Timber frame: at a vertical post, which is the best case, because a frame's upright IS a natural module boundary. Plastered: the hardest — a flat surface has no natural seam, so the edges must be perfectly complementary or carry a deliberate feature at the joint.**

**An outer corner turns the wall away — you see two front faces meeting at a vertical line. An inner corner turns it toward you — you see the inside of the angle, which is in shadow.** **It is harder because the occlusion runs up the full height of the join, making it the darkest part of any wall — and in this projection an inner corner shows more of the top face than a straight run does, so the coping turns.**

Roofs.front: How a roof is drawn in this projection
Roofs.back: **A large sloped plane drawn as a foreshortened top face: the ridge is a horizontal line at the top, the eaves a horizontal line at the bottom overhanging the wall, and the field between is the foreshortened slope with horizontal courses.** **Courses 3–5 px deep with a one-pixel darker line between them — that line is the shadow cast by the overlap, which is occlusion.** **Individual tiles are not drawn; two or three vertical nicks per course suggest them, offset from the course above.**

Roofs.front: Why roof silhouette beats roof texture
Roofs.back: **A slate roof has a crisp straight ridge and a thin eaves line; a thatched roof is thick, rounded and overhangs deeply.** **At 3 × 3 scale that silhouette difference reads from across the screen and the course texture does not.** Slate `TERR-017`–`020`, crisp regular courses. Thatch `TERR-029`–`032`, soft and thick with no courses and a rounded ridge. Timber shingle `TERR-033`–`036`, between the two.

Roofs.front: The two roof problems to raise
Roofs.back: **1 The roof hides the wall, which is a gameplay question** — a roof removed or faded when the player enters, a cutaway, or interiors drawn without roofs. **§9.1 names "interior pieces" in the modular class, which implies interiors are seen — so raise it, because the art depends on the answer.** **2 Height: an 88 px door means a wall of 100 px or more, and a pitched roof foreshortened to half adds 30–50 px, so a house is 130–150 px — about two character heights, and far too big for a 112 × 112 frame. A building is a scene assembly, not one sprite.**

Doors, windows and openings.back: **§9.2: "Door opening | at least 88 px clear | architecture-defined".** **The derivation: an 80 px adult must pass through, so 88 gives 8 px of headroom — which is 17 cm at 45.7 px per metre, and tight. A character in a hat needs all of it.** An opening's five parts: **the reveal (the recess's side faces, visible because the wall has thickness), the lintel or arch, the threshold or sill, the dark interior, and the door itself as a separate piece because it opens.**

Doors, windows and openings.front: The reveal is what makes an opening an opening
Doors, windows and openings.back: **A flat dark rectangle on a wall is a painted rectangle. The fix is one or two pixels of the wall's own material, in Shadow and Deep, inside the opening's edge** — the wall's thickness seen at an angle. **With the light upper-left: the wall's Shadow down the left inner edge, Deep down the right, Deep under the lintel (the deepest occlusion on the whole wall), and `TERR-001`–`002` for the interior, not pure black.** **About six pixels of work, and it is the difference between a window and a hole in a sticker.**

Doors, windows and openings.front: Make the opening a separate piece
Doors, windows and openings.back: **A wall run is repeated sections and an opening interrupts it — so either a wall section with an opening in it, or the opening as a separate piece that REPLACES a wall section.** **The second is better, because then one door piece works in any wall of the same height rather than one door-in-wall piece per wall material** — **which means it must match the wall's thickness, coping and base line, so it is designed WITH the wall, not after it.** That is §9.1's transition seam test.

Gates, fences and posts.back: **A wall is a solid plane and the drawing is the surface. A fence is posts and rails with air between them, so the drawing is the silhouette and the background shows through** — **the one architectural piece where §10.1's negative gaps clause is the whole asset.** Which means **it must read against every background: grass, earth, a crowd of corpse puppets.** §9.2 gives 41–50 px high, 1 tile deep, and §6.8 needs one: *"Four York defenders brace the fence."*

Gates, fences and posts.front: A fence's structure, and its shadow
Gates, fences and posts.back: **A post 2–3 px wide and 41–50 px tall, with a visible top (a small ellipse or 2 × 1 rectangle). Two or three rails, 2 px tall, running between posts. Post spacing one or two tiles — 16 px is a dense palisade, 32 px a field fence. The gaps between rails are the background.** **And the shadow is a row of small ellipses, one per post, not a line along the whole run — because the rails do not touch the ground.** Cheap, and it reads immediately.

Gates, fences and posts.front: Why a fence's rhythm is not the repetition failure
Gates, fences and posts.back: **A fence is inherently periodic, and that is correct — a real fence has evenly spaced posts, so the periodicity is the subject.** **The test changes: not "can I see the repeat" but "does the repeat look like a fence or like a tiled texture".** **And the answer is to vary the pieces, not the rhythm** — a leaning post, a missing rail, a weathered one every fifth or seventh piece. **§9.3's wear caution applies: §6.8's fence is being braced against a press of bodies, so damage there is motivated and elsewhere it is not.**

Floors and interiors.front: Interior floors, and the line that shapes a room
Floors and interiors.back: **Beaten earth `021`–`024`, the quietest possible. Timber boards `033`–`036`, one-pixel lines every 4–5 px with staggered ends. Flagstones `013`–`016`, irregular blocks with mortar. Rushes `029`–`032`, dashes in random directions. And the floor's job is the same as the ground's: quiet.** **The wall-to-floor line is the single most important pixel row in an interior** — one pixel of the floor's Deep or `TERR-002`, two in a corner, **turning at the corners where the deepest occlusion in the room is.**

Floors and interiors.front: Why interiors make the restraint clause obvious
Floors and interiors.back: **§10.1's upper-left key is the AUTHORED light and applies indoors as outdoors — but indoors the real light comes from a window or a fire, which is a `Light2D` at a specific position.** **So an interior is the clearest case of the restraint clause: the baked upper-left key is almost wrong indoors, and it is kept anyway, because consistency matters more and the runtime light supplies the truth.** **Bake the upper-left key, keep it weak, and let the hearth light the room.** Note the interior face of a wall is a different piece from the exterior face.

Cliffs and elevation.front: The three devices a cliff needs
Cliffs and elevation.back: **1 The face is a front face** — a vertical surface with its own material and vertical striations, darker than the ground above. **2 The top edge is a lip** — a one-or-two-pixel band of the ground's Light step along the top, projecting slightly, **which is what reads as an edge rather than a colour change.** **3 The bottom edge is a contact line** — Deep where the face meets the lower ground, plus scree if the material warrants it. **And a cliff needs its own terrain set, because top, face and base are three tile roles plus corners.**

**A low step or kerb at 4–8 px** — one piece plus corners, reads as elevation without a face set, **and it is enough for most of what York needs.** **A retaining wall** — the wall set reused; a wall is a cliff with a tidier face. **A slope or ramp** — a foreshortened top face with a value gradient, **and it is walkable, which avoids the collision question entirely.** **Or no elevation at all** — §9.1 names cliffs because a ramp's Intended uses mentions them, not because the Prologue needs one.

Cliffs and elevation.front: The ambiguity that cannot be drawn away
Cliffs and elevation.back: **A tall cliff face occupies screen height, and the ground at its top is drawn at the same scale as the ground at its bottom, because §9.1 says floors do not converge. So two points one above the other on screen are indistinguishable from two points at different heights.** **No amount of shading fixes it.** What games do instead: **keep elevation changes small and local, use collision to make the geometry unambiguous in play, and accept that a 2D top-down game's verticality is schematic.** §4: *"The camera never rotates"* — so the ambiguity is permanent.

The screen's colour budget, applied.front: A York exterior, curated to 37 colours
The screen's colour budget, applied.back: **Neutral 3 steps; earth 2 (ground is quiet); olive 2; stone 4; timber 4; slate 4; ochre 3; living green 3; moss 2 — nine ramps, 27 colours. Plus a character's skin, cloth and leather, about 10. Total about 37, inside §9.3's 32–40.** **And notice how it got there: the quiet materials use two steps and the structural ones use four** — stage 6's contrast scale applied as a budget.

The screen's colour budget, applied.front: The three ways a scene goes over budget
The screen's colour budget, applied.back: **1 Every material uses all four steps** — nine ramps × 4 = 36 before the characters; the fix is that a flat ground material needs two. **2 Too many ramps** — two greens and two greys where two might do; ask whether the distinction is load-bearing. **3 An identity colour has leaked in** — §9.3's warning that *"identity colours such as Beacon cyan, Grace gold, veil violet and ember are used only when their meaning is genuinely present"*. **A brass hinge in Grace Gold spends an identity colour and makes it mean less when it is used deliberately.**

What is open work.front: Decided against open, for environment art
What is open work.back: **Decided: the projection; the 16 px tile and 8 px subgrid; the four asset classes; the four modular tests; the anchor, footprint and visible-size rules; the eleven per-asset checks; the 32–40 screen budget; the lighting direction and restraint.** **Open: the transition grammar; the environment material ramps; the York calibration assets (§9.2's bands are *"starting calibration, not approval"*); destruction states; VFX rules — plus whether roofs are removed or faded and what is seen through an opening, which §9 does not address at all.**

What is open work.front: How to proceed where the grammar is undecided
What is open work.back: **1 Draw the smallest thing that tests the decision** — one 16-tile edge set and one 16-tile overlay set, for one boundary, so the choice has evidence. **2 Keep it in gitignored `media/work/`** and not a master until the decision is made. **3 Record what you chose and why**, with the six elements of a proposal. **4 Raise it rather than deciding it** — §2.1's *"surface the gap instead"*, with Master Roachi's decisions first and Timon having final say on design. **Where a question is open, the useful contribution is to make the decision cheap to make.**

The eighty-pixel problem.front: What 80 pixels buys, and what it forbids
The eighty-pixel problem.back: **A bounding box of about 85 × 40, about 1,600 pixels occupied, about 1,350 interior after the outline. The head is 10–14 px tall, so the face area is about 6 × 6 = 36 pixels, an eye is one pixel or none, and a hand is two or three pixels across.** **So there is no face — there is a head-shape with room for two dark pixels.** **And the project's answer: one face mark, `#408190`, on s, se, e, w and sw, not on the back views.**

**Draw the silhouette until the character is recognisable in solid black. Only then draw anything inside it.** **Because §10.1 says identity cannot depend on hue, glow, jewellery or microscopic detail — so it is carried by four things: silhouette, equipment that breaks the outline, value structure, and costume shape.** **And a sprite that fails the black test has to be redrawn from the silhouette; no amount of interior work will save it.**

Proportion at eighty pixels.front: Where Shepherds sits on the head-count scale
Proportion at eighty pixels.back: **Academic realism is 7.5 heads (a 10.7 px head at 80 px); heroic 8 (10 px); stylised 6 (13.3); cartoon 4–5 (16–20); chibi 2–3.** **The reference's 10–14 px head on an 81–87 px figure is 6 to 8 heads — the realistic-to-stylised boundary, matching §2's "warm, earthy, weathered" rather than cartoon.** **And it follows from §10.1: identity may not depend on microscopic detail, so there is no point buying face pixels.**

Proportion at eighty pixels.front: The vertical landmarks on an 84 px figure
Proportion at eighty pixels.back: **Crown 84. Chin about 72, so the head is 12 px. Shoulder 68. Mid-chest 60. Waist 52. Hip and crotch about 42 — HALFWAY. Knee 22. Ankle 4. Sole 0.** **The halfway hip is the one landmark worth memorising: the crotch is at half the figure's height in every proportional system and at every scale. Get it right and the figure reads; get it wrong and no detail helps.**

**Shoulder width 18–22 px — roughly a quarter of the height, or two head-widths. Waist 12–15. Hip 14–18. Head width 8–11. Upper arm 4–5 thick, forearm 3–4, thigh 6–7, calf 4–5, ankle 3.** **An upper arm four pixels thick has room for ONE value boundary** — so a limb at this scale is a two-value shape with an outline. **And the variations that distinguish characters: ±6 px of height, ±3 of shoulder, ±2 of head size, ±1 of limb thickness are all visible.**

The head.front: Why hair is the largest identity carrier
The head.back: **It is the outermost part of the silhouette's top, and the top of a silhouette is what the eye reads first.** **What reads: the mass and its outline** — a bun, a tied-back tail, a hood, a hat's brim, cropped, loose. **What does not: strands.** Budget **20 to 50 pixels**, which is a lot at this scale and worth spending. **And it changes by direction — a tied-back tail is invisible from the front and prominent from behind, which is part of why the back views are distinguishable at all.**

The head.front: The head in four directions is four drawings
The head.back: **South: a rounded shape, widest at the cheekbones, narrowing to a chin, with the face area central. East or west: a DIFFERENT shape entirely — the brow and nose project forward, the skull's back projects back, the jaw is visible; not the south view rotated. North: a rounded shape with the hair's mass and the neck, and NO face. The diagonals are genuinely in between, which is where the eight-direction cost is highest.**

**Width 3–4 px, 2–3 px visible — and its job is the occlusion under the chin, because the head overhangs the neck.** **One pixel of Deep there does more for the head than anything inside it, and without it the head sits directly on the shoulders and the figure reads as hunched.** The head's drawing order: **silhouette including hair → black test → neck and occlusion → two values on the face mass → two on the hair → the face mark if the direction has one → stop.**

Hands and feet.front: What a hand can be at three pixels
Hands and feet.back: **A hand is 2–3 px across and 3–4 long — about 8 to 12 pixels. It can be a cluster slightly wider than the wrist, a value distinct from the sleeve, a silhouette that changes when it grips, and a position that reads as open or closed. It cannot be fingers, a thumb, or a gesture.** **And the rule: a hand's meaning comes from where the ARM puts it. Gesture is an arm problem.** When gripping, **the object is what reads, not the grip.**

Hands and feet.front: The foot is a direction cue
Hands and feet.back: **South: foreshortened, 3–4 px long, pointing down-screen, both visible. East or west: full length, 5–6 px, pointing sideways, the near foot overlapping the far. North: foreshortened, pointing up-screen — and you see the heel rather than the toe. Diagonals: one foot more foreshortened than the other.** **So the feet are one of the clearest direction signals in the whole figure, and getting them wrong makes a direction read as the wrong one.** And the foot's job is ground contact: **its lowest row sits at the pivot's row.**

Silhouette first.front: Building a figure silhouette in six passes
Silhouette first.back: **1 The box** — an 85 × 40 rectangle with the ten landmarks marked, on a non-exporting layer. **2 The masses** — head, torso, pelvis, four limbs as simple blocks; check the halfway hip. **3 The contour** — one continuous outline following the masses, smoothing where the body smooths. **4 The hair and the costume's silhouette** — where the character becomes a specific person. **5 The equipment that breaks the outline.** **6 The gaps** — armpits, between the legs, under a strap.

Silhouette first.front: The figure's proportions are not a free choice
Silhouette first.back: **`media/README.md`: the body-part reference idle is "the final reference for every character's idle" and "Every future character's idle animation follows it".** **So the silhouette's proportions are specified by an approved asset** — open a reference frame as a reference layer and draw over it. **And the honest identity standard: put four heroes' silhouettes side by side in black and name each. If you cannot, the design does not distinguish them — which §2.1 and `characters.md` own, not the drawing.**

The eight directions.front: What each of the eight views shows
The eight directions.back: **`s` — the face, chest, both arms' fronts, both feet foreshortened: the most informative view, usually drawn first. `se`/`sw` — three-quarter, face partly turned, one shoulder nearer, the far arm partly hidden. `e`/`w` — profile: the profile head, one side of the body, the near arm overlapping the far, feet at full length; the MOST different from south. `ne`/`nw` — three-quarter from behind, one cheek at most. `n` — the back of head and body, no face: the least informative.**

The eight directions.front: Why eight drawings and not one rotated
The eight directions.back: **1 The head changes shape** — a profile head is not a front head rotated; the brow and nose project and the skull's back projects. **2 Occlusion changes** — in profile the near arm hides the far one; in front both are visible. **3 The light does not rotate** — the key stays at the upper-left while the body turns, so the LIT SIDE OF THE BODY changes: facing south the right shoulder is lit, facing north the left one is.

The eight directions.front: The frame count, and the contract's three mitigations
The eight directions.back: **The idle alone is 8 × 24 = 192 drawings; the run 8 × 12 = 96; and §6.1 lists roughly fifteen action families for Eli — well over a thousand frames for one character's Prologue requirements.** **Which is why §5.3 says requirements come from actual gameplay actions, not speculative sheet lists. The three mitigations: not every action needs eight (§6.1's "south-facing lying/get-up sequence"); not every action needs 24 frames (§5.4 authors to gameplay timing); and the Prologue needs no separate run, with guard, parry, hurt, downed, revive, victory, Shepherd Light and Ultimate all deferred.**

Why mirroring is banned.back: **1 Handedness** — the reference's limb colours are side-tied, *"so a flipped west would swap them"*; and for a real character the handedness is in the costume and equipment, so a flipped sprite holds the crook in the other hand, visibly. **2 The lighting** — the key is upper-left and a flipped sprite's is upper-RIGHT, **so it reads as wrong even on a perfectly symmetrical character.** **3 Action geometry** — an attack's sweep direction reverses, which may contradict the gameplay's hit geometry.

Why mirroring is banned.front: What the runtime actually does about mirroring
Why mirroring is banned.back: **`authored_sprite_body.gd` uses "a west-side tag as drawn, unmirrored, whenever the set has one" and mirrors "only a direction with no drawing of its own".** **So the engine supports both: draw eight and it uses eight, draw five and it mirrors the three it lacks.** **Which means mirroring is a FALLBACK, not a prohibition — a first pass at five directions is a legitimate increment, and §5.4's rule is about what gets APPROVED, not about what the engine can play.**

**"Mirroring is permitted only for an explicitly approved asset whose handedness, costume and action geometry survive the flip."** All three must hold: **no held object and no asymmetric body; no satchel on one hip, no strap over one shoulder, no asymmetric hem; and a symmetrical action.** Plus **"explicitly approved" — a decision, not a default.** **A plausible candidate: a sheep.** Symmetrical, no costume, no handedness — and §6.3 needs directional walking, so the saving is real.

What five directions costs.back: **Draw `s`, `n`, `e`, `se`, `ne` and flip to get `w`, `sw`, `nw` — five drawings instead of eight, a 37.5% saving, which across fifteen action families is enormous.** `s` and `n` are drawn once because they are their own mirror. **What it gives up: handedness, lighting direction, costume asymmetry and action geometry in three of eight directions. What it does NOT give up: the silhouette, the proportion, the timing, the value structure.**

What five directions costs.front: Four questions to decide eight or five
What five directions costs.back: **Does it hold or carry anything? → eight. Is the costume asymmetric? → eight. Is the action asymmetric? → eight for that action, even if the idle is five. Is it a hero the player will watch for twenty hours? → eight, because §10.1's identity clause is about heroes.** **None of the above → five is defensible, and §5.4 requires it to be explicitly approved.** **And the decision is per asset, action AND direction, because that is the granularity of §3.1's masters.**

**Five now, eight later** — the runtime mirrors only a direction with no drawing of its own, so adding `w` later is used immediately at no mechanical cost, and it gets a playable character sooner, which `CLAUDE.md`'s one-asset-at-a-time rule favours. **Eight for the idle, five for everything else** — the idle is what the player sees most and an attack lasts 0.3 seconds, and both approved references are eight. **The risk: a character whose crook changes hands depending on direction is worse than one that is wrong consistently.**

The 81 to 87 pixel variance.back: **Idle: s and n 81 px; se, e, w and sw 84; ne and nw 87 — a 6-pixel range on an 81-pixel figure, 7.4%. The crouch is 6 px lower.** **Run: s 72, se and sw 75, e, w and n 78, ne and nw 81, with a lowest pose of 63 — an 18 px compression.** §4 cites it: *"pose and authored direction may change the measured height. The approved idle reference deliberately reaches 81–87 px by direction."*

**"None of the following is a defect. All of it was seen in the preview and kept on purpose: the 3 px drop when the loop returns from frame 24 to frame 1; the height changing by direction; the few pixels that change during west's hold; east and west starting their crouch one frame earlier than the others. Timon rejected re-timing the key poses and evening out the heights."** **Three lessons: "approved" means someone looked at it in motion and decided; do not fix it, because every future idle follows it; and the standard is "reads correctly", not "measures consistently".**

Anatomical scale across poses.back: **§4: "A pose that crouches, falls or lies down keeps the same anatomical scale as its upright pose. Never normalize each frame's bounding-box height independently; doing so makes prone bodies grow."** **The mechanism: an upright figure's box is 84 × 20; a lying one is about 70 × 24. A tool that scales each frame to the same bounding height blows the 24-px-tall lying figure up to 84 — three and a half times its real size.** **Which is what an automated conversion or a per-frame trim-and-recentre does.**

Anatomical scale across poses.front: The pivot is a world position, not a body part
Anatomical scale across poses.back: **For a standing figure the feet are at the pivot; for a lying figure the feet are at one end of the body. The practical answer: draw the lying figure so (56, 96) is the character's GROUND POSITION — roughly under the torso — and keep that convention across every prone frame, so the get-up animation is continuous at the pivot.** **Which is why the canvas has 16 rows below the pivot: room for a crouch, a fall, a jump's shadow and a prone body.** §6.1 sidesteps most of it by requiring only a **south-facing** lying sequence.

Ground contact.front: The four things that make a foot look planted
Ground contact.back: **1 The foot's lowest row is at the pivot's row — row 96. 2 A line of Deep under it — occlusion, about eight pixels of work for the single largest readability gain available. 3 The contact shadow, on its own layer. 4 And the foot does not move between frames unless the character is stepping** — §4's *"Ground contact must be stable in every frame"*. **The technique: copy the planted foot between frames rather than redrawing it.**

**1 The foot drifts** — the character appears to slide. The standard is "stable", not "identical": the reference permits *"the few pixels that change during west's hold"*. **2 Both feet leave the ground** — correct in a jump or pounce, wrong in an idle; and **a walk has at least one foot down in every frame, where a run has a flight phase.** **3 The shadow moves with the body** — which is why §3.1 gives it its own layer: **it stays on the ground and shrinks as the body rises.**

Ground contact.front: The 13-pixel drift in the run reference
Ground contact.back: **`media/reference/Animation/README.md`: "the recipe anchors each frame on its own bottom-centre, so across a stride the figure's paste column moves by up to 13 px (e and w) as the legs open and close" — and it was "Seen and left alone".** **That is exactly the foot-drift failure, and it survives because the reference is a MOTION reference and not a production master.** **A character's own run must not do that.**

Signature equipment.front: Why equipment is the second-strongest identity carrier
Signature equipment.back: **§10.1: "allow signature equipment to break the torso silhouette" — a permission, not a requirement.** **It is the only interior-of-the-figure detail that survives the black test, because it is not interior: it is OUTLINE.** From §6.1's Eli: **the crook** (a long diagonal projecting above the shoulder and below the hip), **the satchel** (*"part of Eli's required costume"*, and Beacon is invisible while carried because it is inside it), **the sling**, a hood or hat, a cloak.

Signature equipment.front: A held object is eight occlusion problems
Signature equipment.back: **A crook in the right hand: facing `s` it crosses the torso in front; facing `e` it is on the near side, fully visible; facing `n` it is behind the body, partly hidden; facing `w` it is on the far side, mostly hidden.** Plus four diagonals. **And this is where §3.1's layer separation and occlusion fight each other: a crook behind the body cannot be a layer above the body.** **The practical answer: equipment on its own layer where it is in front, drawn into the body layer where it is behind — so the layer split is not uniform across the eight directions.**

Costume as identity.front: What a costume can carry at eighty pixels
Costume as identity.back: **A silhouette change — a cloak, long coat, wide hem, hood — 20 to 60 px: reads strongly, the best investment. A value block — a dark tunic against light trousers: reads, and survives greyscale where hue does not. A hard edge — belt, collar, cuff, hem, 1 px each: reads as a boundary. A large pattern — two or three 2 px marks: marginally. A small pattern or an insignia: no.** **The hierarchy: outline, then the value split, then the hard boundaries, then two or three folds, then nothing.**

Costume as identity.front: The line between a drawing decision and inventing a fact
Costume as identity.back: **§2.1: "Art must not invent costume details, insignia, equipment, anatomy or lore to fill a gap; surface the gap instead" — and "Generated images, old character sheets, filenames, imported assets and text embedded inside an image establish nothing by themselves."** **Every drawing involves thousands of decisions no document will specify, so the line is whether the decision ASSERTS SOMETHING ABOUT THE WORLD.** A fold's position does not; **a crest, a uniform, a scar or a wedding ring does.** And the 2026-09-22 reset put almost all existing art outside the approval boundary.

The four-legged body.front: The Prologue's four animals, in pixels
The four-legged body.back: **At 45.7 px per metre: a sheep 1.2 m long and 0.9 m at the shoulder → 55 long, 41 at the shoulder. A lamb 27. A border collie 25 at the shoulder, 41 long. A roe deer 32 and 55; a red deer 55 at the shoulder. A fox 18 at the shoulder, 32 long.** **The fox is less than a quarter of the human's height — and §6.5 needs six action families from it: worry/pacing, rear, lunge, settle/recover, struck reaction and flee. That is the hardest animation problem in the Prologue.**

The four-legged body.front: What distinguishes the four in silhouette
The four-legged body.back: **Sheep: the fleece's lumpy mass — a cloud on four short thin legs with a small head low down, and a wide body. Dog: the head's size relative to the body, the ears and the tail — a long low body, a lifted head, pricked or folded ears, a plumed tail. Deer: the LEGS — very long, very thin, with the neck held high; mostly legs and neck. Fox: the TAIL — nearly as long as the body and thick, with a sharp muzzle and pricked ears.** **At 18–41 px those four signals are almost the entire drawing.**

**Front legs: shoulder, elbow (bending BACKWARDS), wrist, foot — with the elbow high and close to the body. Rear legs: hip, stifle (bending FORWARDS), hock (bending backwards), foot — and the hock is the distinctive joint, bending the opposite way from a human knee and sitting low.** At this scale a leg is **2–3 px thick and 10–20 px long with two visible joint bends.** **And the error is drawing all four legs the same: front and rear bend in opposite directions, and that difference is visible even at 3 px thickness.**

Timon's reference as a specification.front: The twelve facts the idle reference fixes
Timon's reference as a specification.back: **8 directions (s, se, e, ne, n, nw, w, sw); no mirroring; 24 frames per direction, looping; 12 fps and 2 seconds per loop; the motion in frames 1–10 with the last pose holding through 24; 3–5 key poses per direction; 112 × 112 at pivot (56, 96); heights 81/84/87 by direction; the crouch 6 px lower; its own 13-colour palette; a face mark `#408190` on s, se, e, w and sw; and four deliberate irregularities, kept.**

Timon's reference as a specification.front: What "follows the reference" does and does not mean
Timon's reference as a specification.back: **Follows it: the direction count and no-mirroring rule, the frame count and timing, the pivot and frame, the number of key poses and the hold structure, the heights by direction, and the 3 px loop drop.** **Does NOT follow it: the 13-colour palette (a character uses Palette v0.1), the body-part colour coding, the face mark's exact colour (`#408190` is not in Palette v0.1), or the figure's build.** **Because it is a motion reference: "how a body moves, not what a character looks like".**

Timon's reference as a specification.front: The reference .aseprite files are not masters
Timon's reference as a specification.back: **"The `.aseprite` starters are a record of the conversion, not masters. Do not edit them here. A character's idle master is still one `.aseprite` per direction under `media/sprites/.../source/`."** And the whole directory is `.gdignore`d — *"Godot never imports it"*. **So: open them, measure them, use a frame as a reference layer — and never edit or save them.** The method: **find the 3–5 key poses and which frames they are, note where the hold begins, draw your character's equivalents at the same frame numbers, inbetween to 24, then check the heights and the loop drop.**

The figure checklist.back: **Before: 1 the reference open as a reference layer. 2 costume and identity read from `characters.md` and canon, gaps raised. 3 the direction count decided.** **Silhouette: 4 the hip at half the height. 5 the head 10–14 px, 6–8 heads. 6 gaps at armpits and between the legs. 7 one or two signature projections. 8 the black test.** **Interior: 9 stage 4's and stage 5's checks. 10 the face mark only where the reference gives it. 11 the foot's lowest row at the pivot, with Deep under it. 12 the contact shadow on its own layer.** **Across the set: 13 eight separate drawings with the light staying upper-left. 14 heights roughly matching 81/84/87, no bounding box normalised.**

The figure checklist.front: The three figure checks that matter most
The figure checklist.back: **The black test** — a figure that fails it has to be redrawn from the silhouette, and nothing else will save it. **The hip at halfway** — the one reliable proportional fact, and the commonest thing to get wrong. **And the reference's proportions** — because they are specified rather than chosen: *"Every future character's idle animation follows it."*

What survives at twelve frames a second.front: Which animation principles survive 12 fps at 80 px
What survives at twelve frames a second.back: **Survive outright: timing, anticipation, staging (which is silhouette) and pose-to-pose.** **Barely: squash and stretch (one or two pixels), arcs (an arc across 6 px is three pixels), secondary action, exaggeration.** **Do not: follow through and overlapping action, slow in and slow out, solid drawing, appeal in the facial sense.** **So animation here is strong poses, well timed, readable in black.**

What survives at twelve frames a second.front: The hold is the principle that matters most
What survives at twelve frames a second.back: **The reference: "The motion is in frames 1–10, and the last pose holds through frame 24" — so 10 frames are motion and 14 are a hold. 58% of the animation is one image.** **Why: an idle that moves continuously reads as fidgeting; a breath is a movement, a pause and a return.** **And it is cheap — ten drawings for a 24-frame animation, which changes the cost of the whole project.**

Keys, breakdowns and inbetweens.front: Why pose-to-pose is the only workable method
Keys, breakdowns and inbetweens.back: **The reference specifies keys — "3–5 key poses per direction" — so the structure is given. The black test applies to poses: you can test a key in isolation and not an inbetween. It is cheaper: draw 4 keys, check them, then fill, rather than discovering at frame 18 that the whole thing is wrong. And eight directions: pose-major lets you draw key 1 in all eight, then key 2 in all eight — which is how consistency across directions is achieved.**

**4 key poses (frames 1, 4, 7, 10) → black-test each → 3 breakdowns → play it, because four keys and three breakdowns is already legible → 3 remaining inbetweens → the hold, frames 11–24, one image. Eleven drawings.** Which matches the reference's *"motion in frames 1–10"*. **And a breakdown does more for the animation than any other inbetween, because it defines HOW the motion gets there.**

**Pose-major is better for consistency — the eight versions of a pose drawn in one sitting with the same intention. `CLAUDE.md` prefers direction-major: "Work one asset, action and direction at a time so each authored animation can be reviewed in Godot before the next family expands."** **The reconciliation: direction-major for the FIRST direction, pose-major for the remaining seven.** Finish `s` completely, review it in Godot, then use it as the specification for the other seven — drawing pose by pose.

The hold, and the two-frame hold.front: Three ways to implement a long hold
The hold, and the two-frame hold.back: **Fourteen copies of the frame — what the reference does, and even its hold has "a few pixels that change". Fourteen linked cels — one image, edited once. Or one frame with a duration of 14 × 84 = 1,176 ms, which survives the import as a relative duration.** **The third is cleanest, with one caveat: it makes the timeline show 11 frames rather than 24, so matching the reference's 24 is safer.**

**"About a third [of the run's 12 frames] are byte-identical to their neighbour: those are Timon's two-frame holds, kept" — so roughly four frames are the second half of a hold, leaving about eight distinct images for twelve frames.** A pose held for 168 ms instead of 84. **Where it goes: the contact pose where a foot hits the ground; the extreme of a wind-up; the impact frame. And NEVER in the middle of a fast arc, where it reads as a stutter.**

The hold, and the two-frame hold.front: Unevenness is what makes animation read
The hold, and the two-frame hold.back: **A 12-frame cycle with every frame at 84 ms reads as a machine. The same cycle with four two-frame holds reads as weight.** **And the reference's own irregularities — the 3 px loop drop, the heights varying by direction, east and west crouching a frame earlier — were all "seen in the preview and kept on purpose", with Timon rejecting "re-timing the key poses and evening out the heights". The unevenness is the life.**

Eighty-four milliseconds.front: Why 12 fps means 84 ms and not 83
Eighty-four milliseconds.back: **Aseprite has no frame rate field — duration is per frame in ms, and playback speed is entirely a consequence of it. Wizard derives the rate as `ceil(1000 / shortest duration)`, with rounding ON by default.** **83 ms → 12.05 → ceil 13: WRONG. 84 ms → 11.90 → ceil 12: correct.** Any duration from 84 to 90 gives 12; 91 gives 11. **And 83 is the natural choice, because 1/12 s = 83.3 ms and Aseprite stores integers — so the obvious thing to type imports at 13 fps.**

**A 24-frame idle at 13 fps is 1.85 seconds instead of 2.0 — 8% fast, against a reference specified as "12 fps, 2 s per loop".** **And `BodyBaseRun.FPS := 12.0` is a hard-coded constant, so a 13 fps import desynchronises from the run.** You would not notice it alone and you would beside a correct one: **two characters idling at 12 and 13 fps drift apart visibly within a few seconds.** **Three fixes: type 84; turn rounding off; or put 84 in the template.**

Eighty-four milliseconds.front: Relative durations, and the shortest-frame trap
Eighty-four milliseconds.back: **`duration = frame.duration / min_duration`, stored per frame — so a 168 ms frame in an 84 ms animation gets a relative duration of 2.0 and plays for two frames' worth. That is how a two-frame hold survives either way.** **And the trap: the SHORTEST frame sets the rate. One frame at 42 ms in an otherwise 84 ms animation makes the whole thing import at 24 fps with every other frame at 2.0 — which plays correctly and is confusing to read. Keep the durations uniform.**

Eighty-four milliseconds.front: When a different duration is right
Eighty-four milliseconds.back: **§5.4: "Frame counts outside the approved idle and movement references are authored to the action's gameplay anticipation, active and recovery timing. Smoothness never overrides responsiveness."** **Worked on §6.5's fox: the 0.22 s lunge is 2.62 frames at 84 ms, so 3 frames would be 0.252 s — 15% too slow. At 73 ms, 3 frames is 0.219 s, which is right, and it imports at `ceil(1000/73) = 14` fps.** **The 0.62 s rear is 7.38 frames, so 7 at 84 ms is 0.588 s — within 5% and fine.**

The twenty-four frame idle.back: **Frame 1: the resting pose, the tallest. Frames 2–5: the descent. Frame 6: roughly the lowest point, 6 px below. Frames 7–10: the rise, to a new resting pose 3 px BELOW frame 1's. Frames 11–24: the hold, 1.17 seconds. Then 24 → 1 is a 3 px jump up.** **So the idle is: settle, pause, snap back — and the 3 px snap is the breath.** The figure sinks slowly over ten frames and recovers instantly at the loop, **which is why it was kept rather than smoothed.**

The twenty-four frame idle.front: Building a new character's idle in ten drawings
The twenty-four frame idle.back: **Open the reference direction as a reference layer → identify its key poses by stepping through frames 1–10 → draw frame 1 at the direction's height → draw the lowest pose 6 px lower → draw the final resting pose 3 px below frame 1 → the breakdowns between those three → the remaining inbetweens to frame 10 → the hold.** **Three keys, two or three breakdowns, three or four inbetweens, one hold — about ten drawings per direction, eighty for the set.**

The twenty-four frame idle.front: What an idle must not do
The twenty-four frame idle.back: **Move the feet** — §4's *"stable in every frame"*; the planted feet are copied, not redrawn. **Move horizontally** — the pivot column does not shift. **Change the silhouette's identity** — the black test applies to every frame. **Loop smoothly** — it specifically does not; the 3 px drop is the point. **Or be smooth at all** — ten frames of motion over 0.83 seconds is deliberate, visible steps.

Three to five key poses.front: What makes a pose a key
Three to five key poses.back: **1 It is an extreme — the furthest point of a movement, not a position passed through. 2 The motion changes direction at it, which is the mechanical definition: descending before and ascending after. 3 It reads alone — the black test applied to a single frame.** **An idle's three keys: the resting pose (frame 1, tallest), the low point (about frame 6, 6 px lower), and the second rest (frame 10, 3 px below frame 1, holding for fourteen frames).**

**The amount of movement** — 6 px is the reference's; a nervous character settles 3 px and twitches, a heavy one 8 px slowly. **The timing** — a low point at frame 4 reads as abrupt, at frame 8 as laboured. **The asymmetry** — weight on one leg, shoulders angled, head tilted. **The secondary motion** — a cloak, a tail, a held object. **And the pose itself** — braced, slouched, alert, weary, which is `characters.md`'s decision. **Three keys is a living idle, five a characterful one, more than five a fidget.**

Three to five key poses.front: Get the resting pose right before anything else
Three to five key poses.back: **It is frame 1, it holds for fourteen frames, and it is what the player sees most — so it is effectively the character's portrait.** **Draw it, run the black test, put it beside the other characters, and only then animate.** **And it IS the standing figure from stage 9** — so stage 9's work is the idle's first key, already done.

The hold and the loop drop.front: What the loop drop actually reads as
The hold and the loop drop.back: **Frame 1 is 3 px taller than frame 10, so the loop jumps the figure up 3 px in one frame — and at 3 × 3 scale that is 9 screen pixels in a twelfth of a second.** **It reads as an inhale: the slow settle over ten frames is the exhale, and the instant recovery is the breath being taken.** **Smoothing it would make the loop a continuous oscillation — a bob rather than a breath.** The insight: **the discontinuity IS the animation.**

**A perfectly cyclic animation has no beginning, so the eye cannot find a rhythm and the motion reads as a machine. A loop with one sharp event has a downbeat, and the eye locks onto it.** **Where to put it: at the loop point, which is free — the frame 24 → 1 transition happens anyway, so making it the sharp moment costs nothing. Or at a contact, like a footfall in a walk, which is the same device.** **And check it with onion skin's "loop through tag frames" on, so frame 1's previous is frame 24.**

The idle in eight directions.front: What must be consistent across the eight, and what may differ
The idle in eight directions.back: **Consistent: the number of key poses and which frames they fall on; the amount of movement (6 px settle, 3 px loop drop); the hold's start frame; the character's identity; and the light at the upper-left — so the LIT SIDE OF THE BODY changes.** **Legitimately different: the height (81/84/87); the face mark (present on s, se, e, w, sw, absent on n, ne, nw); the occlusion; and the crouch's start frame, by one, in e and w.**

**Assemble the eight resting poses into an 8-frame animation — s, se, e, ne, n, nw, w, sw — and play it slowly. The character appears to turn on the spot, and any inconsistency in height, build or costume shows up as a jolt.** **The most useful consistency check and the least obvious.** The others: all eight versions of key 1 in one image at 300%; the eight heights measured; the eight silhouettes in solid black side by side; and walking the character in a circle in Godot.

**The reference ships one: `body-base-idle-8dir-contact-sheet-2x.png` — "all 8 directions, 24 frames each, one sheet".** **Making your own is the review artefact: Aseprite's Export Sprite Sheet at 2× by rows, or the command line.** **It is the only way to see 192 frames at once and spot a direction that drifted.** **And it is not an asset** — §3's rule deletes *"temporary conversion material"*.

The twelve-frame run.back: **8 directions, no mirroring. 12 frames, looping, with about a third byte-identical to their neighbour — Timon's two-frame holds, kept. Timing "Not given", played at the idle's 12 fps. 112 × 112 at (56, 96), scale 1.0 = 3 × 3 per art pixel. Heights: s 72, se and sw 75, e, w and n 78, ne and nw 81; lowest pose 63. Face mark on e and w only.** **And it is "an approved motion/body reference, not Eli's final character art".**

The twelve-frame run.front: Why the run is shorter than the idle
The twelve-frame run.back: **The idle is 81–87 px; the run is 72–81 — a running figure is 6 to 9 px shorter, because a runner leans forward and bends their knees. And the lowest pose is 63 px, 18 px below the tallest: a very large compression.** **Twelve frames at 12 fps is one second per cycle, which is slow for a run** — but §6.1 says the Prologue uses one normal movement speed and needs no separate run, **so this is the walk as well, at which speed one second per cycle is reasonable.**

The twelve-frame run.front: The twelve frames as a cycle
The twelve-frame run.back: **Two steps, six frames each. Frame 1: contact, the leading foot strikes — a candidate for a two-frame hold. 2–3: the down phase, the body at its lowest. 4: passing, body at mid-height, the free leg passing the planted one. 5–6: the up phase, pushing off to the highest. 7: contact, the other foot. 8–12: the second step.** **So the height curve is lowest at 2–3 and 8–9, highest at 5–6 and 11–12 — two full oscillations per cycle, which is why a run bobs twice per stride.**

**"Seen and left alone: the recipe anchors each frame on its own bottom-centre, so across a stride the figure's paste column moves by up to 13 px (e and w) as the legs open and close."** **That is the bounding-box normalisation §4 warns about, horizontally — and it was left because the reference is a reference and not a master.** **Your run must keep the pivot column fixed: the hips stay at column 56 and the legs move around them.**

The waist split.front: How the waist split is made
The waist split.back: **Master Roachi, after playing it: "divide the top half of the body from the legs, so that the legs turn toward the direction of movement, and top half of the body goes toward aim but with a restriction on turn."** **The upper half is head, face mark, chest and arms; the lower half is the legs; and "there is no hip colour, so the chest's lowest band is the waist".** At runtime: **the legs play in the movement direction and the upper half, same frame, from the direction nearest the aim, at most two steps away, "moved so its waist lands on the legs'".**

The waist split.front: The three authoring constraints the split creates
The waist split.back: **The two halves come from DIFFERENT directions of the same frame number — legs from `e`, upper body from `ne`. So: 1 the waist must be at the same height in every direction, or the upper body sits too high or low. 2 the torso's width at the waist must match across directions, or there is a step at the join. 3 anything crossing the waist is a problem** — a belt is fine, but a long coat, a satchel strap, a sash or a hem below the waist is drawn in one half and must work against either.

The waist split.front: Why the two-step constraint is acceptable
The waist split.back: **Two of eight steps is 90 degrees, so a character running east can aim from north-east through south-east — and beyond that the body does not twist that far.** **And the clause that makes the clamp acceptable: "The true aim remains represented by the ground arrow" — so the sprite does not have to show the exact aim, because a separate UI element does.** **The implementation: draw the legs and upper body on separate layers and import with `SpriteFrames (Split By Layer)`** — which means the layer structure for movement animations is decided by this requirement.

Anticipation, active, impact, recovery.back: **Anticipation: the MOST, 40–50% of the action — it has to be seen and understood, and a one-frame wind-up is unreadable. Active: the FEWEST, one to three frames — a fast movement IS few frames, and drawing more makes it slower, not smoother. Impact: one or two, often a two-frame hold. Recovery: 30–40%, and it can be interrupted.** **The instinct is to spend frames on the swing, and the swing should be two frames: an action's readability is almost entirely in its anticipation.**

**§6.5: "The lunge currently lasts 0.22 seconds and the rear 0.62 seconds; art must be authored against the gameplay timing rather than redefining it."** **The rear is the anticipation — nearly three times the lunge, which confirms the budget. At 84 ms the rear is 7.38 frames → 7; the lunge is 2.62 → 3, but 3 frames at 73 ms is exactly 0.219 s.** **So: 7 frames of rear, 3 of lunge at 73 ms, and 4 or 5 of recovery — about 15 frames, of which 7 are the wind-up.**

**§5.3 names it separately from the impact, because the impact happens to the TARGET and the release is on the thrower** — §6.1's *"sling throw, sling charge and charged throw"* and *"crook-heavy wind-up and release"*. **Why it must be exact: the projectile spawns at that frame in the game, so a release drawn one frame late shows the projectile appearing before the arm has thrown it.** **The release frame is a gameplay fact, and the animation must match it — not approximately.**

Gameplay timing is the authority.back: **A smoother animation means more frames, which means a longer action, which means a longer delay between input and effect — and that is worse in a game than a coarse animation, because the player FEELS the delay and only SEES the coarseness.** **So a 3-frame lunge over in 0.22 s beats a 6-frame lunge taking 0.44 s, even though the second looks better in isolation.** **And at 12 fps with two-frame holds, coarse is the house style anyway — nobody is expecting smoothness.**

Gameplay timing is the authority.front: The frame-count conversion table at 84 ms
Gameplay timing is the authority.back: **0.08 s = 1 frame. 0.17 = 2. 0.22 = 2.6 → 3 (or exactly 3 at 73 ms). 0.25 = 3. 0.33 = 4. 0.5 = 6. 0.62 = 7.4 → 7. 0.75 = 9. 1.0 = 12.** **The rule of thumb: 84 ms gives you multiples of 0.084 s, so round to the nearest frame and accept up to 5% error — or change the duration when the timing is precise.** **And only three frame counts are predetermined: 24 for the idle, 12 for movement, and everything else is arithmetic.**

One-shots and the underscore.back: **§5.3: "Locomotion and idle cycles loop. Attacks, interactions, reactions, downing and other one-shot actions do not."** **Loop, no prefix: `idle_s`, `move_ne`, `graze_s` (the sheep), `pace_w` (the fox), `sleep_s`, `scamper_se`, `alert_s` (the deer).** **One-shot, `_` prefix: `_crook_attack_1_s` ×3, `_crook_heavy_windup`/`_release`, `_sling_throw`/`_charge`/`_charged_throw`, `_dodge`, `_stoop`/`_hold`/`_rise`, `_lie_down`/`_get_up`, `_bark`, `_dig`, `_sniff`, `_rear`, `_lunge`, `_struck`, `_flee`, `_shove`.**

**§6.1's "sling charge" is the interesting case: a charge is held until released, so it is either a loop or a one-shot ending in a held frame.** **The answer is TWO animations: `_sling_charge` as a one-shot wind-up, then `sling_charge_hold` as a loop** — which is what the gameplay needs, because the player holds the button. **And that is the general pattern for any held action: a one-shot into a loop.** Sleep and alert both loop, because a sleeping animal does not stop sleeping.

**A death animation without it loops: the character dies, and dies, and dies. A dodge without it dodges continuously.** **And it is silent — the import succeeds, the animation plays, it just never stops.** **Which makes it a validator check: extend "exactly one lower-case snake-case tag" to "and the prefix matches the action's classification".** **Note the prefix is on the TAG, not the filename: `eli_dodge_e.aseprite` contains the tag `_dodge_e`.**

Telegraphs.back: **§5.3: "Telegraphs must read through pose, silhouette, motion and sound rather than colour alone."** **Pose: a pose the creature has in no other state — §6.5's fox "rear as a clear dodge telegraph" — because the player learns it once and recognises it thereafter, and a wind-up resembling an idle is not a telegraph. Silhouette: the outline differs sharply, and a reared fox at 18 px becomes 28 px of height, which at that size is the whole signal. Motion: fast movement into a held pose reads as "about to". Sound: `audio.md`'s, and the channel that works when the creature is occluded.**

Telegraphs.front: The telegraph's length is a gameplay number
Telegraphs.back: **The anticipation phase IS the telegraph — they are the same frames — and the response window is the anticipation's duration. §6.5's fox gives the player 0.62 seconds to see the rear and dodge.** Five steps: **find the gameplay duration → convert to frames → draw the extreme pose and black-test it against the neutral → two or three frames into it, then hold the rest → test it in Godot at speed, in a scene.** **Step 5 is the only one that matters: a telegraph that reads when you are looking for it and not when you are playing has failed.**

Secondary motion.front: Secondary motion at 12 fps is a one-frame lag
Secondary motion.back: **Parts that move because the body moved — cloth, hair, a held object, a tail, a strap, a cloak — and they LAG, reaching their extreme after the body does. At 12 fps the lag is one frame. That is the whole technique.** **The three worth animating: a cloak or long garment (2–4 px at the hem, the largest secondary mass and it changes the silhouette); hair (1–2 px, and on a 12 px head that is a sixth, so less is more); and a held object — the crook, 1–2 px at the far end, which is the most effective, because it projects beyond the silhouette.**

Secondary motion.front: Secondary motion is the first thing to cut
Secondary motion.back: **It costs a layer, a pass over every frame, and it is invisible at a glance — and §10.1's priority puts "decorative detail" last, behind silhouette, value separation, pose readability and ground contact.** **Animate the crook because it is in the silhouette; leave the folds.** And do not animate: every fold of cloth (no room, reads as noise); a belt, cuff or collar (attached, no lag); **the feet** (§4's stable ground contact); or a satchel beyond one pixel.

Easing and arcs in pixels.back: **A 6-frame movement across 8 pixels gives you spacings of 1,2,2,2,1 — which is easing, just barely.** **1,2,2,2,1 reads as eased both ends, the standard. 1,1,2,3 accelerating — a fall, a swing's active phase. 3,2,1,1 decelerating — a settle, a recovery. 2,2,2,2 linear — mechanical, correct for a machine and wrong for a body. 4,1,1 a SNAP — fast then held, which is what the reference's loop drop is.** **And the snap does the most work: fast movement into a hold reads as intention, and it costs two frames.**

Easing and arcs in pixels.front: How much arc fits in a pixel grid
Easing and arcs in pixels.back: **A hand moving 10 px along an arc of radius 10 deviates from the straight line by about 1.3 px at the midpoint — so a 10-pixel movement has ONE pixel of arc in it, and it is worth placing.** **Arcs matter most at the hands and the ends of held objects, because they are furthest from the joint: a crook's tip moving 20 px has 3 or 4 px of arc, which is genuinely visible.** **The rule for both: vary the spacing by one pixel at the ends, and offset the midpoint frame by one pixel off the chord.**

**Easing's purpose is to make a movement feel physical; a hold achieves the same thing differently, because a pose held is a pose with weight.** **And holds are cheaper: a two-frame hold costs nothing and reads immediately, where an eased six-frame movement costs six drawings and reads subtly.** **Which is why the reference uses holds heavily — four two-frame holds in a 12-frame run, and a 14-frame hold in a 24-frame idle.** **So: holds first, easing second, arcs third.**

The four-legged walk.back: **Left hind, left fore, right hind, right fore — and diagonal pairs do NOT move together in a walk.** That order is what quadrupeds actually do, and it keeps three feet on the ground at all times, **so a walk has no flight phase.** **And it is the one thing that reads wrongly if wrong: an animal moving its diagonal pairs together is TROTTING, and the difference is visible.** In a 12-frame cycle the footfalls are at frames **1, 4, 7 and 10** — evenly spaced three frames apart, each a candidate for a two-frame hold.

**Vertical: 1–2 px of rise and fall, twice per cycle, as each diagonal pair supports. The shoulder and hip move independently — the shoulder dips when a foreleg is airborne, the hip when a hind leg is. The head nods, 1–2 px. And the tail swings, lagging.** **At 18–41 px tall, 1–2 px of vertical movement is 3–10% of the animal's height, which is plenty.** **And the far legs are often a step darker, which separates them from the near pair.**

**A planted foot is stationary relative to the WORLD, so it moves backwards relative to the body at exactly the animal's speed. The failure is drawing the planted foot as if attached to the body, so it slides forward.** **The check: pick one foot and follow it frame by frame — while down, its horizontal position moves backwards by a consistent amount; when it lifts, it swings forward faster.** **And in a cycle animated in place, the planted foot moves backwards across the frame and the body stays centred. The engine moves the sprite.**

The gallop, and the other gaits.front: The four gaits, and which animal needs which
The gallop, and the other gaits.back: **Walk: four separate beats, no flight phase. Trot: two beats, diagonal pairs together, brief flight. Canter: three beats, asymmetric. Gallop: four beats, gathered and extended, two flight phases.** **The sheep needs a walk only. Pip needs a walk and a run/scamper. The deer needs a run only — §6.4 says it "does not require an ordinary walk cycle" because it is repositioned between sightings. The fox needs a pace and a flee.** **§6.4's economy is the model: ask what the scene actually shows.**

**Gathered (all four legs tucked under) and extended (fore legs forward, hind legs back) — both airborne, and a galloping animal is off the ground for roughly half the cycle, so those two poses are the ones the eye reads.** **8 frames is enough at this scale; 12 is generous.** **And the extended pose is the money shot: at 32 px long that pose is 40 px long — squash and stretch, in the one place it survives.** **A scamper is different: two beats, the hind legs pushing together, with 4–6 px of bounce on a 25 px dog.**

Pip, the sheep, the deer and the fox.back: **§6.2: "curled sleep, idle, walk, run/scamper, nose-down sniff, bark, dig, three-bite chain and dodge."** Plus: **"Dodge is a distinct action from pounce. Pounce is an Act I requirement rather than a Prologue requirement."** **So nine families now, not ten — and those two sentences are the contract reducing the count.** Roughly 400 frames at eight directions where needed.

Pip, the sheep, the deer and the fox.front: The sheep's and the deer's economies
Pip, the sheep, the deer and the fox.back: **The sheep (§6.3): two families only — "idle/graze and directional walking because gathered sheep follow Eli and may face any direction reachable by their movement".** The shortest list of the four, **and the best mirroring candidate: five directions with an explicit approval saves 36 frames.** **The deer (§6.4): four families — graze, notice, alert/watch, depart/run — and NO walk cycle, because "It is repositioned between authored sightings". Only the departure "must support all eight".**

Pip, the sheep, the deer and the fox.front: The fox's six families, and why it is the hardest
Pip, the sheep, the deer and the fox.back: **§6.5: "worry/pacing, rear as a clear dodge telegraph, lunge, settle/recover, struck reaction and flee" — with two exact timings, 0.22 s and 0.62 s, and "art must be authored against the gameplay timing rather than redefining it".** **Six families on an animal 18 px at the shoulder — the hardest animation problem in the Prologue.** **And the four animals together are about 21 families and roughly 700 frames, before Eli's fifteen and the residents' idles** — which is why §10.2's derivation rule is the most valuable clause in the contract.

Beacon, and animating an object.front: Beacon's three states and six awakening beats
Beacon, and animating an object.back: **§6.6: "Beacon needs inert, awakening and awake states. Awakening includes trembling, seams, rings rotating into alignment, rising, flash and settlement. Awake Beacon uses light and a subtle bob. Beacon is spherical and does not require character-style directional facings."** **So: `inert` (a dark sphere, `TERR-105` or no cyan at all), `_awakening` (a one-shot of six beats, perhaps 20–30 frames), and `awake` (a loop, `TERR-107` with a 1–2 px bob over 12–24 frames).** **Six beats, in order, is a complete storyboard.**

**A band rotating around a sphere at 16–24 px: its apparent width changes as it rotates — widest face-on, a line edge-on — and it is occluded by the sphere for half its travel.** **So draw the POSITIONS, not the rotation: six or eight hand-drawn positions, cycling.** **At this scale a ring can be three pixels wide and its rotation read from its vertical position and curvature alone.** **And "rotating into alignment" means the rings STOP — so the cycle decelerates, which is the easing lesson's 3,2,1,1.**

**No directions (spherical — a saving of eight to one). No ordinary ground contact, because it rises, so the contact shadow is its own animation, staying put and shrinking. No anatomy, so the animation is entirely about the object's mechanism — hinges, rings, seams, levers, flames. And it is a light source, so it has no shadow side and the light it casts is `Light2D`'s.** **The beats come from the mechanism's description, and §9.3 requires the states defined before drawing.**

The animation checklist.back: **84 ms — not 83. 24 frames for an idle, with motion in 1–10 and a hold to 24. 12 frames for movement, with about four two-frame holds. 8 directions, authored, no mirroring.**

**Before: the standing figure finished; the gameplay timing known; the frame count derived; the tag name decided with its prefix.** **While: keys first and each black-tested; 3–5 keys for an idle; anticipation gets the most frames; holds on the contacts; the planted foot copied; the pivot column fixed; no bounding box normalised; the light staying upper-left.** **Numbers: 84 ms; 24 or 12 frames; the heights matching the reference; the loop's discontinuity deliberate.** **End: played at 100% and 300%, and in Godot against the real ground under light.**

**At twelve frames a second and eighty pixels, animation is strong poses, uneven timing and deliberate stillness. Draw the keys, hold them, and let the discontinuities do the work.** Pose-to-pose because keys are testable. The 14-frame hold because stillness reads as breath. Two-frame holds on the contacts because uneven timing is weight. The 3 px loop drop because a loop with no event reads as a machine. **Anticipation over the active phase, because readability is in the wind-up — which is what "smoothness never overrides responsiveness" says too.**

UI art is not pixel art.front: The format and pipeline of UI art
UI art is not pixel art.back: Transparent **`.png`**, imported by Godot's own texture import — **not `.aseprite`, and not through Aseprite Wizard**. §3: UI art *"does not inherit sprite canvas, pivot or animation rules"*.

UI art is not pixel art.front: Why UI art is drawn large and scaled down
UI art is not pixel art.back: `hud.md`: *"Large painted UI textures are **downsampled** with a high-quality filter to approximately the pixels they occupy and cached; **they are never enlarged** past their useful source resolution."* The inverse of the sprite rule against resized source art.

UI art is not pixel art.front: Which stage 2–10 rules survive into UI art
UI art is not pixel art.back: **§8's legibility at four resolutions, §10's eight conditions, `hud.md` §11's eight verification items, and the world's visual identity.** The canvas, pivot, four-value rule, no-anti-aliasing rule, 12 fps and Aseprite itself all drop away.

The rendering split.front: The two render paths, in one line each
The rendering split.back: **The world:** a 960 × 540 `SubViewport` enlarged by an **integer factor with nearest filtering**. **The interface:** lifted into the window and rasterised at **native display resolution**, keeping 960 × 540 layout coordinates.
The node that **owns the render split**. It *"sets the window font oversampling to the interface scale while leaving the world viewport pixel-scaled"*.
So that **gameplay measurements stay stable across resolutions** — a HUD element at (480, 520) is bottom-centre at every resolution — **while the rasterisation is still resolution-native**.
