*"**Running a world scene without the shell is not a valid presentation-quality HUD review.**"* The downsample, font oversampling, interface transform and letterboxing all live in the shell.

The rendering split.front: The world vignette's place in the layer order
The rendering split.back: **Over the world and below the HUD**, as an interface layer. It follows the leader's drawn position and `WorldClock.darkness()`, and *"never changes world time or replaces gameplay lighting"*.

The approved HUD family.front: The entire approved art in the repository
The approved HUD family.back: **All UI art under `media/ui/{hud,menu,map,fonts}/` except `inventorywindow.png`**, plus **Timon's two body-part references** (the 24-frame idle and the 12-frame run). Nothing else, as reset 2026-09-22.

The approved HUD family.front: The accepted HUD family, by role
The approved HUD family.back: **Main frame** `timon-frame-v3.png`; **health bar** `character-health-bar-v2.png`; **dash-charge orb**; **dialogue text box**; **minimap border** `minimap-border-compass-v2.png`; **six NPC markers**; **inventory-slot art**; and the font **AlegreyaSC-Bold**.

The approved HUD family.front: Why version numbers in UI filenames do not break the no-archive rule
The approved HUD family.back: Because **only the current version is on disk** — there is no `v1` or `v2` beside `timon-frame-v3`. The number is part of the name, and the superseded files were deleted as §3 requires.

The approved HUD family.front: What replaced the generated party portraits
The approved HUD family.back: **A generic code-drawn silhouette**, until approved portraits exist. The generated portraits were removed entirely under the 2026-09-22 reset.

The main frame as a specification.back: Its **central plate occupies about 52% of the 960-unit frame width** and is **centred on the bottom edge**; *"decorative ornaments may extend beyond the plate without changing the functional layout"*.

**Six numbered plaques** = the equipped active skills; the slot **above** them = **Unity**; the slot **below** = **experience**; the **left** round button opens the menu on **Journal**, the **right** on **Map**.

The main frame as a specification.front: How the frame's round buttons are hit-tested
The main frame as a specification.back: *"Hit testing uses **the painted circle, not its rectangular bounds**."* So the painted circle's centre and radius, in layout units, are facts the code needs.

**Eight painted candles in the frame art**, lit by **one shared transparent 3D viewport**. Each flame aligns to its wick, fades with the HUD, and **leans opposite the leader's acceleration**. *"This isolated effect does not establish a 3D art pipeline for the game world."*

Nine-slice and scalable borders.back: **`NinePatchRect`** — a Control node with `patch_margin_*`, for one specific panel. **`StyleBoxTexture`** — a theme resource with `texture_margin_*`, for every panel of a type. A shared menu shell wants the second.
**Twice the margin plus one pixel.** A border with 8-unit margins cannot draw a panel narrower than 17 units.

Nine-slice and scalable borders.front: Why a nine-slice's centre should be plain
Nine-slice and scalable borders.back: Because **the centre stretches on both axes**, so any detail in it smears at large sizes. Keep it flat, keep it a subtle texture, or set the axis stretch mode to **Tile**.

Painted openings and hit targets.back: **A hole in the HUD art through which code-drawn content shows** — a resource orb's fill, a skill plaque's icon, the experience slot. Its position and size in layout units are **shared facts between the art and the code**.

Painted openings and hit targets.front: The three kinds of art-to-code agreement a HUD needs
Painted openings and hit targets.back: **A fill region** (code draws inside painted art), **an anchor point** (code positions relative to the art — the candle wicks), and **a hit area** (code tests input against a painted shape).

Painted openings expose their fill; text sharp and contrasting; world-to-interface anchors stay on their actors; focus and click targets match the painting; minimap and world input map correctly; **no telegraph depends on hue alone**; leader and companion states readable in combat; subviewports inside the frame budget.

Legibility at four resolutions.back: **The locked viewport (960 × 540), and 1080p, 1440p and 2160p presentation.** The first is layout space rather than a display resolution.

Because **the world's integer scaling and the interface's native rasterisation diverge most there** — the world is scaled 2× and letterboxed while the interface rasterises at 2.67×. Which is why input must account for *"the world viewport, interface transform **and window letterboxing**"*.

Legibility at four resolutions.front: The minimum source scale for UI art
Legibility at four resolutions.back: **4× the layout size**, because 2160p rasterises the interface at 4× and the art is *"never enlarged past their useful source resolution"*. **4× to 8× is the practical range.**

Legibility at four resolutions.front: Why mixing painted and pixel art in one interface layer fails
Legibility at four resolutions.back: Because the interface transform scales the whole layer — so at 1440p the pixel-art part is scaled **2.67×, with filtering, and loses its pixels**. Invisible at 1080p, where 2× is an integer; visible at 1440p.

The placeholder, and what to replace it.back: **The one unapproved file in `media/ui/`** — *"loaded today but explicitly placeholder art"*. §11's first open art item is to replace it.

The placeholder, and what to replace it.front: Why replacing the inventory window is a design job
The placeholder, and what to replace it.back: Because the menu is **one shared shell with eight tabs** (Journal, Party, Codex, Inventory, Stats, Skills, Map, System), needing a nine-sliced frame, openings for different page contents, and **a greyed non-interactive state** for pages unavailable in combat.

**High-resolution pixel portraits** — pixel art, above gameplay resolution. §2 permits *"higher-resolution art than gameplay sprites, but none is currently approved"*. A third medium between the 80 px sprites and the painted UI.

Map markers, and icons at small sizes.back: **`!` and `?`, each in gold, red and silver.** The art exists; the semantics do not — §12 wants *"explicit offered/accepted quest state before treating `!` and `?` as final semantics"* and red markers *"when those systems exist"*.

Map markers, and icons at small sizes.front: The two techniques that work on a 12-pixel icon
Map markers, and icons at small sizes.back: **A dark one-pixel outline**, because the background behind it is unknown; and **one accent value plus one dark value and nothing else** — a third value at that size blurs rather than clarifies.

Map markers, and icons at small sizes.front: Why three hues in one glyph is a §11 failure
Map markers, and icons at small sizes.back: *"No telegraph depends on hue alone."* Gold, red and silver `!` markers differ only in hue, so the distinction fails in greyscale. **Shape — a different glyph, outline weight or badge — is the reliable fix.**

The eight open HUD items.back: Today the charges only **reorder**, so a spent charge is communicated by position rather than by appearance. §12 wants *"a visible spent dodge-charge state"* — **a drawn empty state in the same position**.

The eight open HUD items.front: Why §12's item 8 is a review rather than a change
The eight open HUD items.back: *"Manually review every orb mode, including the restricted state."* The orbs are the HUD's most state-heavy element, and **§2's rule means that review has to happen through the shell**.

The eight open HUD items.front: Which open HUD items are blocked on design rather than art
The eight open HUD items.back: **Items 5 and 6** — the offered/accepted quest state and the red secret markers. The marker art already exists; the meaning does not, and §2.1 forbids inventing it.

The five visual registers.front: The locked principle of the visual system
The five visual registers.back: *"The game uses **multiple visual languages by design**. Their unity comes from **assigning each one a clear narrative role** and **grounding all of them in the same canonical world and character designs**."*

**1** normal dialogue — high-resolution pixel portraits; **2** important staged conversations — in-engine cinematics; **3** heightened sequences — illustrated graphic-novel tableaux; **4** act transitions — fully produced cinematics, which *"may move beyond pixel art"*; **5** Shepherd and metaphysical events — the sacred register.

The five visual registers.front: Which registers Aseprite is actually for
The five visual registers.back: **1 and 2**, plus register 5's pixel-art instances. Register 3 is illustration, register 4 may leave pixel art entirely, and **the painted UI is outside the list altogether**.

The five visual registers.front: What must survive a change of register
The five visual registers.back: **The canonical design** — and at 80 px stage 9 said that is **silhouette, equipment and value structure**. A portrait, a tableau and a cinematic all have to carry those forward to be the same character.

The sacred and the dissonant.front: Sacred versus dissonant, in one rule
The sacred and the dissonant.back: **The same violet family (`TERR-117`–`120`).** Sacred carries a **Sacred White / Grace Ivory core (`TERR-101`–`104`)**; dissonant *"never carries a white core"*. **Look for the white.**

The sacred and the dissonant.front: Why the white core is a better telegraph than a hue change
The sacred and the dissonant.back: Because it is a **value structure rather than a hue**, so it survives §11's *"no telegraph depends on hue alone"* — and it is the same solution stage 5 gave for materials: value carries the information, hue carries the identity.

The sacred and the dissonant.front: Why violet is restricted in the world and exempt in the UI
The sacred and the dissonant.back: Because violet is **a narrative signal**, and a signal that appears decoratively stops signalling. The UI is not the world, so it is exempted — along with lavender flora and Nix Green.

**A distinct technological interface vocabulary** for the one character whose presence is technological — the locked principle applied to a character instead of a scene. Its direction is set; nothing else about it is.

Shepherd Light, Beacon and fire.front: The three questions any effect family must answer
Shepherd Light, Beacon and fire.back: **Where does it attach? What does it respond to? What is its budget?** The candles answer all three — wick, HUD fade plus leader acceleration, one shared subviewport inside the frame budget. Shepherd Light answers none of them yet.

Shepherd Light, Beacon and fire.front: What is actually decided about Shepherd Light
Shepherd Light, Beacon and fire.back: **Only its colours** — violet `TERR-117`–`120` with a mandatory Grace Ivory core. **Shape, animation, duration and layering are all open.**

Shepherd Light, Beacon and fire.front: Why world fire cannot be drawn yet
Shepherd Light, Beacon and fire.back: Because it depends on **§9.3's open lighting and time-of-day treatment**, which is undecided — and §2.1 says to surface that gap rather than invent around it.

Effects at twelve frames.front: The frame shape of an effect
Effects at twelve frames.back: **Anticipation 1–2 frames, the strike exactly 1, dissipation 3–6** — about 5 to 9 frames, or 0.4 to 0.75 s at 12 fps. **Front-loaded, uneven and terminal** — the opposite shape to a looping run cycle.

Effects at twelve frames.front: The three ways an effect differs structurally from a character animation
Effects at twelve frames.back: **It usually does not loop**, so its tag takes the `_` prefix; **its anchor is its own** rather than the (56, 96) pivot; and **it is often directionless or rotated** rather than drawn in eight directions.
**A core, a body, an edge and a halo.** The eye reads the core-to-halo progression as light. The sacred register already fixes the first two — Grace Ivory core inside a violet body.

**The palette.** An additive effect's on-screen colour is **the sum** of the effect and what is behind it, so it is not a palette colour and a strict validator would reject it. Whether to use it is open.

The UI and VFX checklist.front: The first question before any interface asset
The UI and VFX checklist.back: **Is this UI art or world art?** UI art is painted, `.png`, native resolution, outside the sprite rules. World art is pixel art under every rule in stages 2 to 10. **Everything else in the stage follows from the answer.**

The UI and VFX checklist.front: The four facts to carry out of the UI stage
The UI and VFX checklist.back: **1** The interface and the world are rendered differently, and that single fact generates every other rule. **2** Both use 960 × 540 layout coordinates. **3** Five visual languages are deliberate, unified by the canonical designs. **4** VFX is the least-decided area in the contract.

The pipeline, start to finish.front: The nine steps from master to playing animation
The pipeline, start to finish.back: **Save → Godot's scan calls the import plugin → it tests `aseprite --version` → it runs Aseprite headlessly for a PNG sheet and a JSON → it parses the JSON → it builds a `SpriteFrames` → it wraps the sheet in a `PortableCompressedTexture2D` and saves a `.res` → it deletes the intermediate PNG and JSON → you assign the `.res` to an `AnimatedSprite2D`.**
Because **the texture is inside it** as a `PortableCompressedTexture2D` and **the intermediate PNG is deleted**. So there is no loose sheet to go stale and no texture reference to break.

The pipeline, start to finish.front: What does not reach Godot from a master
The pipeline, start to finish.back: **Layers** (flattened, unless split), **blend modes** (baked into the flatten), **the palette** (the sheet is RGBA), and **onion-skin settings, grids, guides and the tilemap structure**. What does: frames and durations, tag names/ranges/directions/repeats, slice names and first-key bounds, and the flattened image.

The command path.back: **Godot's Editor Setting** holding the Aseprite executable's path — on this rig `/home/masterroachi/Games/steam/steamapps/common/Aseprite/aseprite`, **written out in full because Godot does not expand `~`**. **Machine-local; never commit it.**

The command path.front: Why the command path is an editor setting and the loop prefix a project setting
The command path.back: **The path names a location on one computer**, so it must not be shared — editor settings are not committed. **The loop prefix, cleanup flag and default importer are conventions**, so they belong in `project.godot` and are shared.

The command path.front: The thirty-second diagnosis for a failed import
The command path.back: **Run the command path with `--version` in a terminal and check the exit code is 0** — that is literally what `test_command()` does. **Then read the Import dock and the Godot output panel**, where the Wizard's logger prints Aseprite's own stderr.

The command the Wizard runs.front: The common Aseprite command line, every export
The command the Wizard runs.back: `-b --list-tags --list-slices --data <out>.json --format json-array --sheet <out>.png <source>` — **batch mode, tags and slices included in the JSON, frames as an array.**

The command the Wizard runs.front: Why hidden layers export by default
The command the Wizard runs.back: Because `only_visible_layers` defaults to `false`, which **pushes `--all-layers`**. So a hidden reference, guide or scratch layer ends up in the export — **which is why the exclusion pattern exists, and why a name is safer than a visibility toggle.**

The command the Wizard runs.front: `--merge-duplicates`, and what it means for holds
The command the Wizard runs.back: **On by default** (except in columns/rows mode): identical frames are stored once in the sheet and several JSON frames point at the same rect. **So a held frame costs a JSON entry and no texture space — holds are free.**

§3 bans *"resized or filtered source art"*, and **the world viewport already integer-scales the whole scene**. Scaling the art too means the art's pixel is no longer the viewport's pixel — breaking §10.1's grammar against every asset that did not do it.

Layers, exclusion and the hierarchy.front: What the exclusion pattern is matched against
Layers, exclusion and the hierarchy.back: **The full layer path** — `Group/Subgroup/Layer`, built by parsing `--list-layer-hierarchy`'s two-space indentation. So `^Reference$` will **not** match a layer inside a group. And it is a **search, not a full match**.

Layers, exclusion and the hierarchy.front: What an invalid exclusion regex does
Layers, exclusion and the hierarchy.back: **Nothing — silently.** `_compile_regex` logs *"Exception regex error"* and returns nothing, so **every layer exports**. An invalid pattern looks exactly like an empty one.
**Name every non-exported layer with a leading underscore and use the pattern `(^|/)_`** — the alternation matches either the start of the path or a slash before the name, so it works at every depth.

Layers, exclusion and the hierarchy.front: The pipeline's most confusing silent failure
Layers, exclusion and the hierarchy.back: **A reference layer exporting.** It flattens over the art, so **the sprite looks right in Aseprite and wrong in Godot.** The diagnosis is one step: look at the exported sheet, not the master.

The JSON the pipeline reads.front: The Wizard's entire validity test for a data file
The JSON the pipeline reads.back: **`is_valid_spritesheet`: a dictionary with `frames`, and a `meta` that has `image`.** Nothing else.
**`keys[0].bounds` — only the first key.** So a slice that moves across frames contributes only its first position: fine for a nine-slice margin or a static anchor, useless for a per-frame hitbox.

The JSON the pipeline reads.front: How to read the JSON when the importer deletes it
The JSON the pipeline reads.back: **Run the Aseprite command yourself, writing into `/tmp`.** Preferable to turning `aseprite/import/cleanup/remove_json_file` off, which leaves a stray sheet beside the master — exactly what §3's one-master rule wants gone.

The frame rate, derived.back: **A twelfth of a second is 83.33 ms, and Aseprite's durations are whole milliseconds.** `ceil(1000/83)` = `ceil(12.048)` = **13 fps**; `ceil(1000/84)` = `ceil(11.905)` = **12 fps**. So 84 produces the contracted rate and 83 is the number that looks right and is wrong.

So that **an animation never plays slower than authored** — a frame is shown for at most its authored duration. Which is the right bias when §5.4 makes gameplay timing the authority. The cost: anything not exactly `1000/n` plays slightly fast.

The frame rate, derived.front: What one short frame does to a tag's rate
The frame rate, derived.back: **It sets the rate for the whole tag.** Seven frames at 84 ms and one impact frame at 42 ms gives `ceil(1000/42)` = **24 fps**, with the other frames becoming relative durations of 2. The animation still plays correctly; the resource just reads 24.

Relative durations.front: How a frame's duration survives the import
Relative durations.back: `var duration = frame.duration / min_duration` — **a multiplier on `1/speed`, not a time.** So at 84 ms minimum, a 168 ms frame has duration 2 and a 252 ms frame has duration 3.
**The animation's `speed`** — frames per second, one number per animation. **Each frame's `duration`** — a multiplier on `1/speed`, one number per frame. Both come from the import.

Relative durations.front: The authoring rule that keeps every derived duration whole
Relative durations.back: **Use only multiples of 84 ms: 84, 168, 252, 336.** Then every division is an integer, the rate stays 12, and the timing is countable in frames — which is what §5.1's 12 fps rule implicitly asks for.

Relative durations.front: The two ways to author a hold, and their cost
Relative durations.back: **Duplicate the frame** (two entries, one merged rect, two frames of duration 1) or **lengthen it** (one entry, one frame of duration 2). Lengthening is usually better; duplicating is right when the held frame is not quite identical — **but it makes a 24-frame idle fewer than 24 drawings.**

Loop, and the prefix that inverts it.back: **`aseprite/animation/loop/enabled` (default `true`) sets the flag; a tag beginning with `aseprite/animation/loop/exception_prefix` (default `_`) has the prefix stripped and the flag inverted.** The Shepherds project overrides neither.

Loop, and the prefix that inverts it.front: Why the Godot animation name is not the Aseprite tag name
Loop, and the prefix that inverts it.back: **The prefix is stripped on import.** A tag `_attack_s` becomes the animation `attack_s`, and the code plays `"attack_s"`. So the prefix is authoring metadata riding on the name, invisible in the game.

Loop, and the prefix that inverts it.front: What an Aseprite tag repeat count does on import
Loop, and the prefix that inverts it.back: `if repeat != -1: is_loopable = false` — **the frames are expanded into that many copies and the loop flag is forced off.** So repeat 3 on a 4-frame tag gives a 12-frame one-shot. **Never how to author a cycle.**

Tag direction and repeat.front: How a ping-pong tag is expanded
Tag direction and repeat.back: **The forward pass, then a copy with the last frame always dropped and the first frame dropped only if it loops, reversed and appended.** So 5 frames give **1 2 3 4 5 4 3 2** looping (8 per cycle) or **1 2 3 4 5 4 3 2 1** as a one-shot.

Tag direction and repeat.front: Why the approved idle is not a ping-pong
Tag direction and repeat.back: Because a 13-frame ping-pong would give exactly §5.1's 24-frame cycle for 13 drawings — **but Timon's approved idle has four kept irregularities and a loop drop, and an irregularity is by definition not symmetric.** A legitimate tool the approved reference rules out.

Tag direction and repeat.front: What a reverse tag saves you
Tag direction and repeat.back: **Drawing the animation backwards.** `frames.reverse()` runs before anything else, so a door closing is the opening tag reversed. **The limit: motion is rarely time-symmetric** — a run's recovery is not its anticipation played backwards.

Static Texture, and the first frame.back: **Default `true` on the Static Texture importer**, pushing `--frame-range '[0, 0]'`. So **frame 1 is the canonical frame of any static asset**, and experiments on later frames are invisible to the import — legitimate scratch space, and a place work gets forgotten.

**The texture the Wizard produces** — it carries its own compressed image data inside the resource, which is necessary because the intermediate PNG is deleted. **Compression mode lossless**, which is non-negotiable for pixel art.

**A meta flag set on every resource the Wizard produces.** So a `SpriteFrames` or texture without it was not produced by this pipeline — a checkable assertion of *"Aseprite Wizard is the only production import/export path"*.

Static Texture, and the first frame.front: Which importer for each of the four asset classes
Static Texture, and the first frame.back: **Characters and creatures → SpriteFrames. Terrain → Tileset Texture (or Static Texture for a hand-laid sheet). Props and set-pieces → Static Texture. UI art → none of them**, because UI art is `.png` outside the sprite pipeline.

Split By Layer.back: **One resource per layer** — the layers are listed, the exclusion pattern applied, and each survivor exported separately with `--layer <path>`, named after the layer with `/` replaced by `_`.

Split By Layer.front: Why trim-cels must stay off under the contract
Split By Layer.back: Because **`--trim` crops each layer's export to its own content**, giving each a different bounding box. §4's canvas and the (56, 96) pivot depend on every export being the full 112 × 112 canvas, so trimmed layers no longer align.

Split By Layer.front: The project's real use for split-by-layer
Split By Layer.back: **Studying Timon's multicoloured body-part references** — one animation per limb, so a single forearm's arc can be read across 24 frames with nothing else moving. **An analysis tool, not a rigging system**: the game's bodies are single flattened sprites.

Split By Layer.front: Why layered sprite assembly fails at eighty pixels
Split By Layer.back: Because **a limb's silhouette changes with every angle**, so a reusable forearm is a forearm drawn for one angle — and **rotating pixel art breaks the pixel grid** while non-integer translation blurs it. Hence whole authored frames: 24 for an idle, 12 for a run, per direction.

Bake files, and the machine without Asep.back: **`.<filename>.ase_bake.res`, hidden, beside the master** — the finished resource saved a second time with the source's MD5 in a `source_hash` meta. **Loaded as the import result when the Aseprite command fails.** Controlled by `aseprite/import/import_plugin/generate_bake_files`, default `false`.

Bake files, and the machine without Asep.front: The bake file's one real risk
Bake files, and the machine without Asep.back: **The staleness check is a warning, not an error.** A mismatched hash logs *"baked file hash does not match current source file"* **and uses the bake anyway** — so a stale bake imports successfully and silently plays the old art.

Bake files, and the machine without Asep.front: Whether this project should enable bake files
Bake files, and the machine without Asep.back: **Not yet.** One author, one machine, Aseprite installed — and bakes double the committed art while adding a silent failure mode. **Turn them on the moment a second machine or a build step needs to import sprites**, and record the decision then.

What a re-import regenerates.back: **Everything.** There is no incremental path: the Aseprite export, the JSON parse, the resource construction and the save all rerun. **So nothing edited in Godot's SpriteFrames panel survives** — not a renamed animation, an edited duration, a toggled loop flag or an added animation.

**`<master>.import`, beside the master and committed** — it holds the chosen importer and the per-file options (exclusion pattern, round fps, sheet type, scale). **It is how one master can use different options from another**, and it survives re-imports.

What a re-import regenerates.front: The one thing a re-import will not fix
What a re-import regenerates.back: **A stale animation name in code.** Rename a tag `_attack_s` → `_strike_s` and the import succeeds while every `play("attack_s")` fails at run time — the character stands still during an attack. **Which is why §3.1's naming grammar is a contract with the code.**

**After any master change; after any project-wide Wizard setting change** (existing `.res` files do not update themselves); **after an addon update**, since the arithmetic could change; **and before a review**, so what you are looking at is what the master says.

The standalone window, and batch work.back: **The automatic importer** — Godot's own import system, the committed repeatable production path. **The standalone window and docks** — hand-picked source, options and output location, for one-off resources and exploration. Plus an inspector dock on `AnimatedSprite2D`.
**`output_location` defaults to `res://`** — the project root. Set it deliberately every time, or litter the repository.

The standalone window, and batch work.front: What to batch and what not to
The standalone window, and batch work.back: **Batch the re-import, never the authoring.** `CLAUDE.md`: *"Work one asset, action and direction at a time so each authored animation can be reviewed in Godot before the next family expands."* The multi-selection reimport is for applying a changed setting across a family that already exists.

Scripting, and a palette validator.front: The sentence that implies a validator should exist
Scripting, and a palette validator.back: `colour-palette.md`: the four cleanup colours `#281E18`, `#241B16`, `#1F1F11` and `#FFFFFF` are ones **"a validator must accept"**. That clause only makes sense if a validator is expected.

Scripting, and a palette validator.front: Which contract checks a script could actually make
Scripting, and a palette validator.back: **Mechanical:** every colour in the palette plus the four cleanup colours; the canvas dimensions; the tag naming grammar and prefix; every frame duration a multiple of 84 ms. **Needs judgement:** four values per material, the violet rule's exemptions, and whether the required actions exist.

Scripting, and a palette validator.front: The Aseprite scripting surface a validator needs
Scripting, and a palette validator.back: **`app.sprite`** with `width`, `height`, `colorMode`, `palettes`, `frames`, `tags`, `layers`, `slices`; **`sprite.frames[i].duration`** in seconds (so 84 ms reads as `0.084`); **`image:getPixel(x, y)`**; and **`aseprite -b --script <file.lua>`** to run it headlessly over many files.

Scripting, and a palette validator.front: The cheapest first step on palette validation
Scripting, and a palette validator.back: **Lospec's free palette identifier and analyzer on an exported PNG** — they do the colour half today without writing anything. The Lua route is worth about fifty lines for the palette and duration checks; the rest should stay human.

The pipeline checklist.back: **1** `--version` from a terminal. **2** the importer set in the Import dock. **3** the Godot output panel. **4** export by hand into `/tmp` and look at the PNG. **5** the JSON's durations. **6** the JSON's `frameTags`. **7** the exclusion pattern against full layer paths. **8** re-import after any setting change.

The pipeline checklist.front: The four facts to carry out of the pipeline stage
The pipeline checklist.back: **1** The shortest frame in a tag sets the rate, rounded up — 84 ms gives 12 fps, 83 gives 13. **2** Every other duration is a multiple of that shortest one. **3** The loop flag is a project default inverted by a prefix. **4** The import is total every time, so the master is the only source of truth.

The two tests, revisited.front: The two tests, and which fails first
The two tests, revisited.back: **The craft test** — can you draw a thing that reads as what it is, at the size it will be seen, within a fixed palette? **The contract test** — can you produce an asset this project will accept? **The contract test is a gate and fails first; the craft test is a ceiling.**

The two tests, revisited.front: Why the constraints are the craft's grammar rather than its obstacles
The two tests, revisited.back: Because **each one makes a decision for you**: at 80 px identity is silhouette, equipment and value structure; at four values form is key, form shade, occlusion and light; at 12 fps motion is three to five poses with holds; within 132 colours colour is a chosen ramp.

The brief, written properly.front: Where each brief field's answer comes from
The brief, written properly.back: **Subject** → `characters.md`, `bosses.md`, canon or the production brief. **States** → §9.3. **Directions** → §5.4. **Actions** → `systems.md`'s accepted actions, and §6 for the Prologue. **Geometry and anchor** → §4. **Palette subset** → `colour-palette.md`. **Runtime consumer** → the node, script and scene, and therefore the importer. **Eight answers, every one findable in a document — so the brief is research, not invention.**

*"**Anything with no accepted on-screen use is not a production requirement yet.**"* It forbids drawing ahead of the design — art for a system that changes is wasted, and art for a system that does not exist invents it.

The brief, written properly.front: Why writing "none" in a brief field is an answer
The brief, written properly.back: Because **it is what stops a prop quietly growing eight directions.** A brief with a blank field invites a drawing decision; a brief that says "none — a prop, one view" has already decided.

The Prologue's actual requirement.back: **Seventeen** — idle; movement; south-facing lying/get-up; stoop/hold/rise; a general interaction; kneel/lift/stow; remove-from-satchel; place-on-bench; three crook-chain attacks; crook-heavy wind-up and release; sling throw, charge and charged throw; dodge; a shove/stagger reaction.
**Guard, parry, hurt, downed, revive, victory, Shepherd Light and Ultimate animations.** Also Pip's pounce, which is an Act I requirement — *"Dodge is a distinct action from pounce."*

**Eli's run** — one movement speed covers the final run north. **The deer's walk** — repositioned between sightings. **Beacon's directions** — spherical. **The crowd scenes** — *"framed shots… rather than full free-movement coverage"*.
**The lunge lasts 0.22 seconds and the rear 0.62** — and *"art must be authored against the gameplay timing rather than redefining it"*. At 12 fps that is 3 frames and about 7.

What later-game adds.front: §7's principle for a hero's animation set
What later-game adds.back: *"Every directly controlled hero ultimately requires **only the animation families their accepted actions use**."* Typically twelve families — including aim-relative locomotion and six equipped active skills — plus hero-specific transformations, equipment, summons and Ultimates.

What later-game adds.front: The two sentences that stop the requirement exploding
What later-game adds.back: *"**NPCs and enemies receive the smallest set their actual behavior requires.**"* and *"**Ambient characters do not automatically receive hero-level directional or combat coverage.**"* The second is the standing exemption for the ten named residents.

What later-game adds.front: Where behaviour is decided versus where it is drawn
What later-game adds.back: *"The owning skill and combat documents define behavior; this document defines how that behavior is visually represented."* And *"boss animation lists follow their finished encounter designs"* — so no boss animation is a requirement until its encounter is done.

What the numbers actually come to.front: The exact floor for one character's two cycles
What the numbers actually come to.back: **288 drawings** — a 24-frame idle and a 12-frame run, each in eight separately authored directions with no mirroring. Not an estimate: it is what §5.1 and §5.2 require.

What the numbers actually come to.front: The single biggest cost lever in production art
What the numbers actually come to.back: **Directional coverage, not frame count.** Eli's fifteen one-shots cost 720–1,200 drawings at eight directions, 360–600 at four, 90–150 at one. **So the most valuable question is "how many directions does this action actually need?"**

What the numbers actually come to.front: The two contract allowances that reduce directional cost
What the numbers actually come to.back: **The ground arrow** carries the true aim, so the sprite's facing need not. **And the waist split** — legs and upper body may differ by up to two direction steps, so one upper-body set can serve several leg directions.

What the numbers actually come to.front: The residents' arithmetic, and its answer
What the numbers actually come to.back: **Ten residents × 24 frames × 8 directions = 1,920 drawings for people who stand in a village.** §6 asks only for *"an appropriate standing idle"*, and §7 exempts ambient characters from hero-level coverage — **so the reduction exists and needs stating in a brief.**

One asset, one action, one direction.front: The working rule, and the argument for it
One asset, one action, one direction.back: *"Work one asset, action and direction at a time so each authored animation can be reviewed in Godot before the next family expands."* Because **a mistake in the first direction is a mistake in all eight** — a wrong pivot, palette, proportion or timing is one file to fix or eight.

One asset, one action, one direction.front: Which direction to draw first, and why
One asset, one action, one direction.back: **South.** The player sees it most, the face is visible, and **it is the hardest** — a forward-facing figure has the least silhouette information, so if it reads the others will. **Approving south approves the character.** A recommendation, not a rule: §6 *"does not prescribe drawing order"*.

One asset, one action, one direction.front: The real tension in the one-at-a-time rule
One asset, one action, one direction.back: **Consistency wants a batch; risk wants a unit.** Eight directions drawn in one sitting are more consistent than eight across eight sittings. **A defensible resolution — keys for all eight, one direction finished and reviewed, then the rest — is a proposal, not an assumption.**

Working with Timon.back: **How it looks → Timon** (final say on design, and all final UI art). **Whether it is acceptable → Master Roachi** (final visual and animation authority, and sole Aseprite author). **What a thing is → the documents.**

Working with Timon.front: What the approved set tells you about the collaboration
Working with Timon.back: **Every approved asset in the repository is Timon's** — the two motion references and all the UI art. The 2026-09-22 reset cleared everything that was not. **The approved set is one person's work, approved because a person made it.**

Working with Timon.front: Why a drawn reference is a better animation spec than a written one
Working with Timon.back: Because **the specification is demonstrably achievable — it was achieved first.** Timon drew the idle and the run, they were approved, `media/reference/Animation/README.md` measured them, and §5.1 and §5.2 wrote the measurements into the contract. A written spec with no reference is a page of guesses.

Working with Timon.front: How to ask a design question
Working with Timon.back: **State what you were drawing and which brief field is blocked; quote what the documents do say; state precisely what is missing; offer a provisional proposal grounded in the established grammar; say what it unblocks.** Do not draw three options and ask which — that converts a design question into a review.

Preparing an asset for review.front: The ten checks to do before a review
Preparing an asset for review.back: **Canvas untrimmed; pivot right; colours in the palette subset plus the four cleanup colours; four values per material; no anti-aliasing, banding or banned dithering; tag names and prefixes right; durations multiples of 84 ms; frame count matching the reference or the gameplay timing; a clean import with the right speed and loop flag; the black and grey tests passing.**
*"Every animation is checked **at native scale**, **in motion**, **against the real ground** and **under representative lighting**."* Set them up before the review, not during it.

Preparing an asset for review.front: Why not to bring alternatives to a review
Preparing an asset for review.back: **A review of three variants is a design meeting**, and §2 puts design with Timon rather than with the review. A genuine design choice is a question to ask before drawing.

**Approved** — it joins §1's list and the document is updated. **Changes requested** — the same master is edited and re-reviewed. **Rejected** — *"deleted rather than archived"*. **Blocked on a design gap** — recorded in the open work, and the asset waits.

Surfacing a gap.back: **A missing canonical detail** (a resident's costume); **a missing design decision** (the markers' semantics); **a missing system** (red secret markers); **a missing technical decision** (lighting and time of day); **and a reduction worth proposing** (ambient directional coverage). The first four are questions; the fifth is a proposal.

**A placeholder is recorded as temporary and explicitly not approved** — `inventorywindow.png`. **An invention answers a design question by drawing an answer, and looks approved because it looks finished** — the generated party portraits, which the reset removed. **The difference is entirely whether it is written down.**

Surfacing a gap.front: Why a surfaced gap should carry a proposal
Surfacing a gap.back: Because **a gap with a suggested answer is a decision somebody can make in a minute**; a gap without one is a task. The proposal must be grounded in the established grammar and marked provisional.

Everything that is open.back: **1** Draw final character, creature, terrain, building, prop, portrait, VFX and remaining UI assets. **2** Replace the menu-window placeholder and the code-drawn party portrait silhouettes. **3** Draw approved terrain and character/creature masters to replace the current code and greybox placeholders.

Everything that is open.front: The project's art state in one sentence
Everything that is open.back: **The rules are settled and almost none of the art is made.** The approved set is UI art plus two motion references; everything else is placeholder, greybox or code-drawn — **which means nothing drawn from here has to be reconciled with a legacy.**

Everything that is open.front: The only open-work row you can act on alone
Everything that is open.back: **"Blocked on nothing but drawing"** — every asset whose brief can be written today: props, terrain tiles, the Prologue's required animations. The other rows wait on a design decision, a missing system, a technical decision, an approved reduction, or Timon.

An order of work.front: The three defensible orders of work
An order of work.back: **By risk** — draw what would most expensively invalidate other work. **By dependency** — terrain first, since everything stands on it and is judged against it. **By playable slice** — everything one scene needs, then the next.

An order of work.front: The two assets worth drawing first, and why
An order of work.back: **Eli's south idle and one terrain tile set.** The idle fixes the proportion system, palette subset, material grammar and value structure for every human; the tile set fixes the ground's value range. **Together they are the first real test of figure against ground.**

An order of work.front: What should come before all of it
An order of work.back: **One complete prop, end to end** — brief, draw, name, import, validate. It exercises the whole pipeline on an asset small enough to throw away. **The project's established pattern: one proof, validated, then production** — as with the pail, the Eli test scene and Timon's two references.

The repository, kept clean.front: Why masters live inside the Godot project
The repository, kept clean.back: Because **the importer is an `EditorImportPlugin`**, triggered by the file being under `res://` — a master outside it cannot be imported automatically. And the alternative, a separate art folder plus exported PNGs, is exactly the second stale artefact §3's one-master rule bans.

The repository, kept clean.front: The five things never to commit
The repository, kept clean.back: **The machine-local command path; intermediate sheets and JSON; rejected or superseded art; an archive folder of old versions; and unapproved art presented as approved.** The one thing easy to miss that *should* be committed: bake files, if ever enabled.

*"**Do not use sequence names** such as `animation1` or `walk2`."* The name is a contract with the code, and a sequence number carries no meaning once the sequence changes. **`<asset-key>_<action>_<direction>`**, always.

Where the craft goes next.front: The four free resources, and what each is for
Where the craft goes next.back: **Slynyrd's Pixelblog** — 64 long-form articles, the best free writing on the subject. **Saint11** — ~90 precise one-technique cards. **Lospec's tutorial index** — 586 tutorials, for breadth and second opinions. **Lospec's palette tools** — the cheapest palette validation there is.

Where the craft goes next.front: The one conflict between the best free resource and the contract
Where the craft goes next.back: **Slynyrd mirrors character sets freely; §5.4 permits mirroring only for an explicitly approved asset whose handedness, costume and action geometry survive the flip.** Read the technique, apply the contract.

Where the craft goes next.front: What this curriculum deliberately leaves out
Where the craft goes next.back: **Pixel Logic** (paid); **the ~25 art books** (reserved for the Drawing curriculum); **drawing itself**; **illustration and the tableau register**; **paint-program UI art** (Timon's); and **3D**, which the candle flames explicitly do not establish a pipeline for.

The contract on one page.front: Every geometry number in one answer
The contract on one page.back: **960 × 540 viewport; 112 × 112 character frame; pivot (56, 96); ~80 px adult, varying 81–87 by direction; 16 px tile with an 8 px subgrid; ~45.7 px per metre, so 1 px ≈ 2.2 cm.** And 112 × 112 is exactly 7 × 7 tiles.

The contract on one page.front: Every animation number in one answer
The contract on one page.back: **12 fps, durations in multiples of 84 ms; a 24-frame looping idle of 3–5 poses; a 12-frame run; eight separately authored directions, no mirroring; legs and upper body at most two direction steps apart; one-shot tags prefixed `_`.**

**Every number in the contract has a reason, and you now know what each reason is** — which is the difference between following a contract and understanding one, and what lets you tell a gap to surface from a rule to apply.
